subtopic: LETTER FROM COMMISSIONER TO MEMBER FOR MELFORT

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LETTER FROM COMMISSIONER TO MEMBER FOR MELFORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 7 last the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), in the course of his contribution to the debate on the address, referred to a matter which he had asked the Combines Investigation Act commissioner to investigate and report on, and expressed his willingness to table the report which was made by the combines commissioner on that occasion. Objection was taken to that procedure upon what seemed to me to be an excellent ground, namely that if we permitted members to file documents of that sort we might find ourselves following the practice of the United States congress in that regard. It was pointed out, however, by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) that if this document were presented by a minister, it would take the curse from it. I am glad indeed to table the document, and I suggest to the house that it be reported completely in Hansard because it deals with a matter which is of great interest now to all the farmers of Canada.
By way of introduction to the tabling of the document, I might perhaps insert in Hansard at this point the information that the hon. member for Melfort had asked the commissioner to investigate and to report upon-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: LETTER FROM COMMISSIONER TO MEMBER FOR MELFORT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, I should like to know under what rule this statement is being made by the Minister of Justice.

subtopic: LETTER FROM COMMISSIONER TO MEMBER FOR MELFORT
speechtext: I understand that earlier in the session a question arose with respect to a report which it was requested should be tabled, and objection was taken to the tabling of the document. The minister now is asking permission of the house to table the document. This is the time at which documents should be tabled. I understand the minister would like to go further and have the document included in Hansard. Am I correct in that understanding?

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LETTER FROM COMMISSIONER TO MEMBER FOR MELFORT
speechtext: That is right, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: LETTER FROM COMMISSIONER TO MEMBER FOR MELFORT
speechtext: Is it the wish of the house that the document should be included in Hansard?

subtopic: LETTER FROM COMMISSIONER TO MEMBER FOR MELFORT
speechtext: No.

subtopic: LETTER FROM COMMISSIONER TO MEMBER FOR MELFORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that this document be printed in Votes and Proceedings. Had it been allowed to be printed in Hansard on the day that I asked that it be printed, I would have commented on the letter at that time to a rather larger extent.
I certainly would consent to its being printed in Votes and Proceedings.

subtopic: LETTER FROM COMMISSIONER TO MEMBER FOR MELFORT
speechtext: Speaking to the point of order, Mr. Speaker, may I say that I objected to the printing of this letter in Hansard, when it was first asked for, on the ground that letters, articles and the like which are not read are not eligible to be printed in Hansard. If documents, letters and newspaper articles are filed and so printed, Hansard will no longer be what it is entitled, namely, House of Commons Debates. With whatever ruling Your Honour may make in connection with the document submitted, for which the minister accepts responsibility, I would not be in conflict. But I respectfully suggest that the printing of letters and other documents received by members or tendered by members would be a wrong practice for us to adopt.

subtopic: LETTER FROM COMMISSIONER TO MEMBER FOR MELFORT
speechtext: Speaking to the point of order, Mr. Speaker, it occurs to me that, the objection having initially been taken to the printing of this letter verbatim in Hansard, it should stand without alteration, otherwise we are going to get into an extraordinary position. If the procedure now suggested by the minister is followed, it will establish a principle under which a minister to whom the letter was not addressed, having received from an official in his department a copy of a letter addressed to another hon. member- here the hon. member for Melfort-is then able to have it tabled. It is not a letter addressed to the minister at all. It is not a document, and I suggest it would be establishing a questionable precedent to allow the minister to have that letter either tabled or printed in Hansard, or in Votes and Proceedings. It seems the letter must come, if it comes at all, from the hon. member to whom it was addressed.

speakerposition: Solicitor General of Canada; Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: LETTER FROM COMMISSIONER TO MEMBER FOR MELFORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if there is any grave objection to the course that is being suggested, I for one am not anxious to press

Printing of Documents in Hansard it. While this document takes the form of a letter in reply to the hon. member for Melfort, actually it is a report upon the questions which the hon. member addressed to the combines investigation commission, concerning a matter of very great interest to the farming industry of Canada. Having regard therefore to its substantial character, perhaps it would be of interest to all members of the house and of public interest generally that it should be tabled and printed in extenso in Hansard. If there is any disposition that that should not be done, I think it will be a very easy matter to inflict a few remarks upon the house and thereby submit the substance of the report in a debate at some appropriate opportunity, and perhaps that is what I should do.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: LETTER FROM COMMISSIONER TO MEMBER FOR MELFORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister may be unduly sensitive about the reception that the house will give to any remarks he may make. I judge that from the words he has just used, but I do not think it should be put upon that basis. When he says that he will then be called upon to inflict some remarks upon the house instead of simply tabling the letter, I would point out that this discussion relates to a ruling which Your Honour made a few days ago, and which should be well understood by hon. members. That ruling applies to members of the government as well as to other hon. members. What was pointed out a few days ago was that unless it is something that falls strictly within the ordinary rules of the house, there are other opportunities which present themselves to introduce into the records of the house any remarks or any part of any document which could be read.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, in relation to the earlier ruling you made, and in respect to what has already been said, that hon. members should be clear on this particular point. Either we are to be permitted to file statements, letters or other material of the kind without their being part of a speech made in the house or fitting into any of the rules which ordinarily apply, or we are going to recognize some established practice which brings them into the usual channels of publication in Hansard.
I suggest that if it is to be the rule that hon. members must avail themselves of some ordinary opportunity in debate to put such material on the record, then that rule should be followed in every case. I do believe it would be unwise to extend the practice of permitting documents to be placed on record without being read. For reasons that are obvious, consent is accorded to the Minister


of Finance in presenting his budget, and to ministers in regard to schedules of figures and information which simply supplement statements they are making in the house; but now that this has come up I think it would be well, Mr. Speaker, if you did draw a distinction between the tabling of schedules of that kind by consent of the house and the suggestion that communications, documents or otherwise should be placed on the record at any time without being read when these simply refer to subjects that could be dealt with in the ordinary course of debate.

subtopic: LETTER FROM COMMISSIONER TO MEMBER FOR MELFORT
speechtext: There are public documents which it is necessary to table, and they should be tabled at this time. I understood the hon. member for Melfort would like to have it included in Votes and Proceedings. Would it meet with the wishes of the house to have this document included in Votes and Proceedings'? Agreed?

subtopic: LETTER FROM COMMISSIONER TO MEMBER FOR MELFORT
speechtext: No.

subtopic: LETTER FROM COMMISSIONER TO MEMBER FOR MELFORT
speechtext: No.

subtopic: LETTER FROM COMMISSIONER TO MEMBER FOR MELFORT
speechtext: It is not agreed?

speechtext:
I for one attach some
importance to the point that was raised earlier as to the origin of the request that this letter be printed in Votes and Proceedings. The point which I think is important is that this being a letter, or having taken the form of a letter, it should only be printed-in any part of the records of this house-on the request of the hon. member to whom it was addressed. speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: DISPOSAL OF TOUGH AND DAMP WHEAT
speechtext:
Is the
Minister of Trade and Commerce in a position to make a statement in regard to the present market position of damp wheat on the prairies, and the prospects of being able to move it from storage so as to make way for the wheat to be threshed?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DISPOSAL OF TOUGH AND DAMP WHEAT
speechtext:
As every hon. member
knows, the problem in connection with tough and damp wheat this year is something far more serious than has ever been met before. We have taken into the elevators about 190 million bushels of tough and damp grain, and we estimate that another 60 million bushels of tough and damp grain is now on the farms ready to be marketed. We are moving that tough and damp grain-giving damp grain the preference-into elevators as rapidly as we can. We believe that that amount of grain-that is, 250 million bushels-can be handled without serious loss, and arrangements are being made which we think will make that possible.
To date about 55 million bushels of tough and damp grain have been dried in the public and private terminal elevators, of which the larger portion is damp grain. Damp grain is now being moved to driers in Duluth, and later on it will be possible to move more damp grain for drying in the United States at other lake ports. We must make it clear, however, that 250 million bushels of touigh and damp grain is all that we can possibly undertake to handle in this crop year.
It is within the power of those who have grain in the fields, by exercising patience, to wait until all that grain can be harvested as dry grain. If they will do that, there will be no difficulty about marketing the grain that has not been harvested. Unless they do
[Mr: Gregg.]
that, we see very little possibility of their being able to market tough or damp grain harvested after the winter months.

maintopic: DISPOSAL OF TOUGH AND DAMP WHEAT
speechtext: What is the estimated amount still on the farms unharvested?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DISPOSAL OF TOUGH AND DAMP WHEAT
speechtext: I believe I gave that figure the other day. I think it was about 140 million bushels.

maintopic: DISPOSAL OF TOUGH AND DAMP WHEAT
speechtext: Can the minister inform us as to the drying capacity in Canadian elevators, per month, and what will have to be moved to the United States for drying?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DISPOSAL OF TOUGH AND DAMP WHEAT
speechtext: I cannot say what the drying capacity in Canada is. We have dried about 55 million bushels in five months, so that I suppose about 10 million bushels a month would be a fair estimate. The amount that we move to the United States will depend upon the capacity for drying that we can have allocated for Canadian grain, and the capacity of elevator space available. We are selling certain grain as tough grain, and moving it as tough grain. Our Canadian mills are receiving only tough grain to mill into wheat, and Great Britain is taking a great quantity of tough grain. As for damp grain in store, which represents our real problem, we believe we will be able to dry it without spoilage. Indeed, our confidence is evidenced by the fact that we are now paying an extra 20 cents a bushel on damp wheat, and damp barley.

maintopic: DISPOSAL OF TOUGH AND DAMP WHEAT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a further question. Will consideration be given to issuing special disease-free certificates to farmers within the quarantined area of Saskatchewan, so that they may be able to ship out tough and damp wheat?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
maintopic: DISPOSAL OF TOUGH AND DAMP WHEAT
speechtext: Yes; those certificates are now being furnished, and they are being accepted at country elevators.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, March 14, consideration of the motion of Mr. E. W. George for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amende ment thereto of Mr. Fair.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: May I bring to the attention of the house the fact that almost daily there is considerable confusion in the house when we enter upon; the orders of the day, and it is most difficult for me to hear what is being said by the hon. member who is speaking. I would ask hon. members who feel that they have pressing duties that require them to leave the chamber to do so as quietly as possible, and also that there should not be conversation at that time to such an extent that I cannot hear what is being said.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before we adjourned on Friday evening I had stated that there wais no disagreement between the C.C.F. and the Liberals regarding democracy's over-all objective in its conflict with communism. While we agree with the point of view expressed by the Prime Minister over the week end that it would be sheer folly to seek to destroy the Soviet state by force, we are prepared, just as are other parties represented
[Mr. Graydon.l
in this house, to resist to the utmost of our ability any further aggression by Russia or by any of its satellites.
Whatever difference of opinion there may be between the C.C.F. on the one hand and the Liberals on the other, it does not concern our objective of preventing further communist aggression, regardless of what form that aggression may take. Such differences of opinion as do exist on this subject are with respect to the method by which our common objective is to be attained. Surely we have not reached a state of dictatorship in this House of Commons whereby one dare not differ with government policy, even on a matter as serious as our conflict with communism, without being charged with aiding the enemy.
Surely it is still possible in this parliament to debate the pros and cons of government policy and in that process discover what the known facts are without being accused of following the Kremlin line. Is it not a fact that is recognized by all of us, including the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), that Russian aggression is not necessarily confined to military aggression? Is it not a well-recognized fact that the economic collapse of France, Italy or any of our European allies would serve the purpose of Russia just as well as or probably better than the military conquest of any of those countries?
Is it not a well-recognized fact that the struggle between democracy and communism in the underdeveloped areas of the world is basically an economic and not a military struggle? Is it not also a well-established fact that our success in holding those underdeveloped areas within democracy's camp will depend on the extent to which democracy can demonstrate to those people that we can provide more security and a higher standard of living than communism can?
If we accept these premises, then surely there can be some difference of opinion regarding the balance that is to be maintained between military preparations, military expenditures and economic security in Europe, and between military expenditures and economic assistance to the underdeveloped countries. Am I not correct in saying that we stand to gain more by debating these questions in an effort to ascertain all the known facts than we would by trying to brush off criticism with the charge that those who criticize the government's policy are aiding the enemy?

The minister reminded us, as reported on page 388 of Hansard of March 13, as follows:
The power of the U.S.S.R. on land, as expressed in terms of divisions, is probably anywhere from 175 to 225.
Newsweek, in its publication Platform, for November, 1950, tells us that General Omar Bradley said that Russia had 175 operational divisions; that they could be increased to 300 divisions within sixty days, and to 500 divisions within a few months of mobilization. Who can tell us how many divisions Russia will have ready by 1954 as compared with NATO's proposed 100 divisions? Speaking of economic and social difficulties, the minister asked this question, as reported on page 390:
If that aggression should occur, then what chance shall we have in NATO, in the United Nations or anywhere else to promote that economic and social progress about which we have all spoken so many times . . . ?
I should like to ask the minister a question which in my opinion is just as logical as the one he asked. If that aggression should occur, then what chance shall we have in NATO, in the United States or anywhere else with 100 divisions in the field against Russia's 300 or 500 divisions, if in the meantime there has been an economic collapse in Italy or France or any other European country? Surely the economic stability of our European allies is a matter closely tied in with our military strength, and one which merits some consideration in this house. It cannot be brushed aside, either by the minister charging his critics with aiding the enemy, or by the Globe and Mail saying that the C.C.F. was talking nonsense when it said that NATO was becoming militaristic and overdoing preparedness.
Preparedness implies much more than military preparedness. Neither the minister nor the Globe and Mail has shown us that in building up our military preparations we are not neglecting other more important aspects of our program of preparedness. Economic assistance to the underdeveloped areas to enable the hungry millions to help themselves to greater production, and a consequent higher standard of living, is placed by the minister as of secondary importance. He placed military preparedness first. There are many well-informed people who consider economic assistance at least of equal importance with military preparedness. It seems to me that we must not neglect either for the other. Probably none of us is in a position to say whether, in the course of future events, economic assistance or military preparedness will prove to be the more
The Address-Mr. Noseworthy effective defence against communist aggression, since none of us is in a position to know just what form that aggression will take.
Another phase of our preparedness program is in the field of propaganda, the battle for men's minds. In a broadcast from Washington on March 4, President Truman made certain statements which appear in . a published pamphlet under the title "Cargo of Truth". He said that the democracies' ultimate victory must be won in the minds of men. He believes that the final solution for the ills that plague the world can never be found in armies, navies or air forces. The final victory cannot be won until truth has made all peoples free. That being so, what is to be gained by a responsible minister charging those who sincerely seek that truth with aiding the enemy? What is to be gained by a responsible newspaper like the Globe and Mail brushing aside our queries with the statement that we are just talking nonsense? , It may well be, as the Globe and Mail says, that 50 divisions are the bare minimum of strength required. Who knows? Is it not much better, and more intelligent, to say that the bare minimum of divisions required is the maximum that the NATO nations can provide without neglecting other facets of our preparedness, and without so weakening the economy of our allies that they may become a ready prey to the enemy? Out of this debate, more heat than light was generated.
There emerged, however, certain facts. The first fact is that the official NATO statement did not mean what is said in plain English. The official statement of NATO says that NATO nations agreed to provide approximately 50 divisions in appropriate conditions of combat readiness during the present year. The minister tells us on page 389 of Hansard for March 13 that those sentences do not mean that by the end of 1952 there will necessarily be 50 divisions ready for immediate action, but that by the end of the year they will be in various stages of readiness, which may mean almost anything.
Mr. Eden, speaking in the British House of Commons, was much more explicit. Mentioning the proposed number of divisions, he said he thought that was a matter that might well be gone into during the debate. I have heard no suggestion from this government that the number of divisions is a subject that we in this house should go into during the debate. Mr. Eden went on to say that possibly the contradiction is due to the fact that of the 50 divisions mentioned only a

The Address-Mr. Noseworthy
certain portion are or were said to be active divisions at present in the line in Germany. A number of these are reservist divisions at various stages of notice. Had the NATO statement not contained the contradictions referred to by Mr. Eden, or had the minister been as frank with us or with his radio audience as Mr. Eden with the British house, much of the acrimony in this debate would have been avoided.
A second fact which has emerged from the debate is that while NATO made provision for increasing the actual military strength of the treaty nations, it reduced the objectives from those which had been secretly set before the Lisbon conference. What has not emerged from the debate, and what the minister has not told us,, is where the additional twenty-five divisions mentioned in the NATO statements are to come from; what nations are to supply them, and in what state of readiness? Above all, I feel we have a right to know what Canada's commitment is, how many of those twenty-five divisions Canada is to provide, and what progress we are making in fulfilling those obligations.
Dean Acheson, in a national broadcast on February 29, which is published under the title of "Strength and Unity", after summing up the five major accomplishments at Lisbon has this to say:
These negotiations will now go on to another stage-one that is familiar to us-one in which these actions will be debated, discussed and acted upon by the representatives of the people in each of these countries. This is as it should be. In our free societies meetings of the ministers cannot be decisive unless they are deeply rooted in the understanding and support of the people and the people's representatives.
It is because of the absence of any such assurance that there will be an opportunity for an early and orderly debate on this subject that we have injected the matter into the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. If such discussion is necessary, as Dean Acheson says, to ensure the understanding and support of the people and the people's representatives of decisions taken by the meeting of ministers, then I submit that these ends will not be gained either by a responsible minister designating his critics as abettors of the enemy, or by a responsible newspaper brushing our criticisms aside as nonsense.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I want to turn to one or two other topics with which I had not time to deal when speaking earlier in this debate. I want to mention a matter which concerns the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), namely, unemployment insurance. In my earlier speech I pointed out the need for an increase

in the payments to those unemployed, the need for a shorter waiting period, the need for some arrangement with local welfare departments under which in cases of distress the unemployed may get advances from the welfare department, to be repaid from the unemployment insurance; and I called attention to the need for one or more additional offices in the metropolitan area of Toronto.
Another matter I think the minister should take into consideration when amendments to the act are being considered is the position of the unemployed who are unable to work because of illness. Those who become ill while unemployed or who are laid off work because of illness have no security under unemployment insurance. Technically speaking I suppose they are then unemployable and are a charge on the local community. It would seem to me that those concerned with the administration of the act should give some consideration to finding a way by which those who have paid into the fund for a period of years may receive some assistance during periods of illness, when they need unemployment insurance or financial assistance much more than when they are well.
There is also need for an overhauling of the basis upon which unemployment insurance is paid, a need for someone with authority to cut some of the red tape and short-circuit the procedure in cases of dire need. It has been suggested to me that a completely new formula for the payment of unemployment insurance might well be worked out. For instance, I understand that in the state of Michigan there is no longer any need to employ enough bookkeepers to look after the affairs of the Canadian National Railways, as is the case with our own unemployment insurance commission; that there is no need to go back five years to check the number of stamps a man has in his unemployment insurance book. When a man becomes unemployed it is conceded that the minimum on which he can exist is $25 a week, and he is automatically paid $25 a week once he establishes the fact that he is unemployed, without any of this business of going back for two, three, four or five years to check on his unemployment insurance stamps. The length of the period during which the $25 a week is paid may be either the time required to find him another job, or whatever length of time it has been decreed that unemployment insurance shall be paid. Some of the Canadian supervisors who have studied that system tell me there is no evidence of abuse but that it has enormously reduced the bookkeeping and

office work, and that it is meeting the needs of the unemployed much better than our own system.
Another matter touching the Department of Labour on which I want to speak briefly is government annuities. As we all know, a bill was before us last session amending that act. Two of those amendments were of special interest to the public, one making the maximum pension allowable $2,400 instead of $1,200 per annum, and the second providing for cash surrender values. The minister undertook during the recess to give us some assurance that the bill would be brought before us again this session, but there is no mention of it in the speech from the throne. On the contrary we are given to understand that the government has made some new discovery, and that the bill may not be brought before us again. It would seem that it is now filed away in the archives.
I think we are justified in asking the government why this amending bill is not coming before us this session, after passing a committee of this house last session. Those of us who followed the work of that committee will recall that there was a bit of a battle. We recall that both the association of insurance companies and the association of insurance agents opposed the bill; and unless it does come before us again this session we can only conclude that the government has succumbed to the lobbying of the insurance people. The Minister of Finance expressed a great deal of righteous indignation about the lobbies carried on by the automobile dealers association and the tobacco companies. I wonder wherein those lobbies differed from the lobby carried on by the insurance companies against the annuities bill. Is it possible that the insurance lobby contented itself with a direct approach to the finance department, whereas the others dared approach members of parliament instead? And are we to gather from this that lobbies, to be successful in the future, must restrict their approach to the Department of Finance? Many of us think that the success of the insurance lobby in this case is only a repetition of the lobby that was carried on in 1948 when interest rates were reduced from 4 per cent to 3 per cent, mortality tables were made more conservative, and other changes were made which caused government annuities to become a little less attractive to the public.
The objection of the insurance companies to these amendments was based on the fact that in their opinion the government was subsidizing these annuities, and as a result that was unfair competition with the insurance
The Address-Mr. Studer companies. I think we should remind ourselves that the public is now subsidizing insurance companies just as much as, if not more than, the public would have been subsidizing these annuities had those amendments been adopted. Every time any member of the public buys an insurance policy or an annuity from an insurance company and pays what is quite evidently an exorbitant rate for that insurance policy or that annuity, he is to that extent subsidizing the insurance company. Certainly a government elected by the people for the purpose of maintaining or protecting the interests of the public should give consideration to the interests of the public and should place them above those of the insurance companies or of any other group. If the government pigeonholes the amendments to this annuity bill, I think it will be quite evident to the public that the government is yielding to the pressures of the insurance companies and is placing the interests of the insurance companies above those of the general public.
There are other matters, Mr. Speaker, on which I had hoped to touch but I have no doubt that there will be another opportunity; I shall therefore deal with them later.

To the best of our ability we endeavour to solve the difficulties of all the people in Canada. That is the only method we can use if we ever wish to make Canada great. So the people in the west- especially those of Maple Creek-wish all the people in the east well.
We in Maple Creek, along with the other people in Canada, mourn for our late sovereign. Along with our sympathy we offer a silent prayer for Her Royal Highness, and we offer a silent prayer for the repose of the soul of our late sovereign. The Address-Mr. Studer goes our sympathy, our love and our devotion. Every person in Canada will be doing his utmost to make lighter the almost unbearable burden that she will be carrying.
On this day, Mr. Speaker, March 17, may I say that I do not believe that it would be just right if we did not offer to the 1,267,702 Irishmen and their descendants in Canada, who today celebrate the feast of their patron saint, our heartiest congratulations on their being lucky enough to have been born Irishmen. I do not know anyone who would not like to be one. All over the world, wherever they may go, they have the reputation of being the most desirable of people. They enter readily into the ordinary life of every nation, and they assimilate themselves so comprehensively that they are almost immediately in the position to make a great contribution to whatever country they adopt. They have great influence. I know of no people that are more patriotic than the Irish or that love more intensely the countries of their adoption. Most countries, for their police, depend on Irishmen more than on anyone else. In my opinion that is the reason why one can give them great credit for being patriotic and loyal citizens, when all the nations of the world place confidence in them to the extent to which they have in depending on them to police their land.
I think the world would be a better one if we had more Irishmen in it. I therefore can only repeat what I said last year namely that Canada will not be able to get along without my constituency. That being the case, all hon. members will be interested in seeing that we, with you with us, make it possible to continue our contributions to the welfare of this country.
As often happens in this country, and especially in our part of it, not all of the people were in a good crop district this year;

but they are making the best of what they have, as we were raised to do. As to our crops that are under the snow, we have not given up in a hopeless manner or in despair. We expect our dominion government to come to the rescue, as I think they will; and we expect our provincial governments to forget their differences, not to try to make professional critics out of themselves in regard to what the dominion government is doing, and to also come to the rescue. Let us all do what we can, both dominion and provincial governments, to enable us to conquer the difficulties that are constantly besetting those who have adopted the vocation of agriculture. Those people have difficulties to contend with which no one else encounters, because these difficulties are beyond their control. Most people in Canada can control, at least to some extent, their operations, their conditions, their futures, their budgets and what have you. The farmer cannot because he is subject to the vagaries of nature. He has to take what nature offers. If in the future we are going to continue to eat, I would suggest that we all give considerable continued thought to and take an interest in the welfare of the farmers of this country.
As to our damp grain, we want all the efforts that governments are capable of in finding a solution for the difficulties. With all of the provinces and the dominion cooperating, I am sure that at least most of that grain can be salvaged. I therefore repeat that I do not think it is the function of either the federal or the provincial governments just to criticize the efforts of one another. I suggest that perhaps it is time to come to the assistance of one another here in Canada if we are going to create conditions which are in the best interests of our people.
We have heard a little about the foot-and-mouth disease in our country. The constituency of Maple Creek, possibly more than any other constituency, supplies the beef of Canada. It is therefore of particular interest to me that no resources of the governments remain untouched in dealing with the problem. It is of particular interest to everyone that a safeguard be thrown around not only the constituency of Maple Creek but the entire province, in order to eliminate that dread disease that has infected or that has infested, one could call it, a $2 billion industry in Canada, to see that that industry be maintained, and that no extensive outbreak occurs anywhere else. Out of 299 municipalities in the province of Saskatchewan, I think we can be grateful that there are only four of them within the confines of this quarantined district. If that is

the record, it seems to me that someone in the livestock branch of the Dominion of Canada, and particularly in the veterinarians branch, must have been doing a very good job to confine the effects of a disease such as that within that area. Whatever criticism is offered-and I think criticism should be offered if it is warranted-I do not think that history will show that the Department of Agriculture was not doing its utmost to confine and to eliminate this particular disease that is prevalent for the time being out in Saskatchewan.
I have heard considerable criticism in the House of Commons in regard to what was done and what was not done. Nevertheless, perhaps it is premature to form an opinion in regard to it. Many hon. members asked: Why was not something done last fall, why was there such a long delay? Suppose an announcement had been made last December that foot-and-mouth disease was prevalent in Saskatchewan. What would 'have been the economic dislocation three months previously to when it was announced? What would have been the effect on the economy of Canada in the last three months, if the announcement had been made earlier? I think the government used good common sense when they made sure that the disease was foot-and-mouth disease before they permitted a condition to come about whereby nations would have imposed embargoes in the same way as they have been imposed by the provinces, with the dislocation that one sees now in evidence. I believe that applies not only to this disease but also to hog cholera which has been prevalent in the United States for years and years. We never hear of it in Canada, and therefore somebody must have been protecting this country, and I think it is the Department of Agriculture. The veterinarians branch and the representatives in the various districts have been protecting Canada throughout these years. If that had not been done we would have suffered greater economic losses than we are experiencing now.
When this criticism is made, we wonder where some of our friends of the opposition were between the last day of November and the day before this house opened this spring. It seems to me that the opposition are supposed to be the watchdogs of this dominion. If they had as much foresight as they have hindsight they would have been talking about this thing during the last session, not during this one. Where were the provincial governments? I said a moment ago that I had made a truce and I was not going to criticize anyone. But where were they during this time? It seems to me they have some responsibility here. The provincial minister of agriculture was down in Mexico from May 29 to June 8, 1951. I am referring to the minister of agriculture of Saskatchewan. He was down there attending some meeting. I have heard a little on all sides recently about redistribution in Canada. I can assure you, on good advice from the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), that a nonpolitical basis of redistribution will be adhered to. No one needs to worry. However, in regard to redistribution, Maple Creek, as you know, is the largest settled constituency in the dominion. It has the largest number of polling places. It has 262 rural polls, which is more than any other constituency in the Dominion of Canada. We are not particularly worried about what is going to happen to us, if we have to lose five seats, because we are in the corner. We are bordered by Montana and Alberta. Medicine Hat does not want us. I have not been able to convince Montana, and as long as foot-and-mouth disease is in our country they will not have any part of us. However, it is a large constituency, and this is one of the problems that Canada is going to have to solve. I do not think the problem of redistribution or representation by population has been solved in Canada up to this time. How can any one member, no matter who he is, represent a constituency that is 180 miles long and 80 miles wide? The people in that constituency

The Address-Mr. Studer demand, expect and have a right to have the same representation as' the people in the city. The city member does not have to travel one mile in order to see his constituents. Just think of the member who has to travel one and a half times around the world, as I would have to do if I followed the road allowances of my constituency, and yet I receive the same remuneration as the member who does not have to travel one mile in his constituency. Is this going to be a country where only the rich can afford to be members of parliament? That is what we are rapidly coming to, because only the rich can afford to be continually on the road, buying new automobiles and trying to get around their constituencies and trying to give service to the people whom they represent.
What are we going to do? Are we going to put a floor under the number of members that each province can have, so that the number will not decrease below that floor? That is true at the present time of Prince Edward Island. Are we going to do that, or are we going to have representation by districts, by areas or by acres rather than by population? I do not think either suggestion is feasible. With respect to those areas that have a small population and still need to be represented, perhaps a combination of the two will have to be the result. I do not know of any other method that we can possibly adopt. Prince Edward Island has a floor of four senators. That province has a population of approximately 100,000. Saskatchewan, which has a population of over 800,000, has six senators. How can there be equality of representation -throughout Canada on that basis? As I see it, the whole structure has to be changed if we are to have any semblance of equality in representation throughout this country.
Far be it from me to say that we should have more senators in Canada. I would suggest that perhaps we can do with a few less.

Because I think they have a balancing influence in Canada that no other

comparable country has. I think they are a valuable stabilizing influence in political affairs. For that reason I think we should keep them. All you need to do is to compare our country with other countries and see what is happening under a system where you elect both houses. If you do that you will see -that the value of senatorships rests on the fact that they are not elected, and that they can view legislation without being subjected to political influence and that drastic political propaganda that we have been subjected to as members during this last while in the House of Commons from special interests trying to gain a point in one way or another. They can disregard that and consider the legislation on its merits. I believe there is some value there, and it should last for a long time. But far be it from me to say that their number should be increased. However it will happen that way, or it will happen so that the number of senators from some provinces will be reduced. If that is not so, what is the answer? If that would not provide equal representation, then let someone else kindly come forward with a plan of his own.
The trend of the times is to have proper agricultural representation. Right here in the House of Commons today only eleven per cent of the members represent the farmers of this country-and when I say "farmers" I mean those who are producing the food, those who are producing the essentials of life, without which one could not get along. One can live without anything else, except food. He can go down to the tropics, and if he did it would not matter whether he had clothes, an automobile, a radio or television- he could get along without any of those. But he could not get along without food.
That is why I say proper representation of the agricultural community is necessary in this country. I am insisting that that agricultural representation be maintained so that our country can prosper, and so that our population can be guaranteed that they will have food. That is essential, and it should be in the minds of all of us. We want our situation with respect to representation to conform to present-day conditions.
I have the utmost respect for that which has passed. The older I get, the more respect I have for history. But when history does not conform to our present needs, then I am afraid some historical changes will have to be made, because what was considered suitable a hundred years ago is I believe unsuitable today, and especially is that true in connection with membership in the House of Commons.

We have a few problems still facing us out west-not only a few, but quite a few- and one of those is the wheat board. We have had some of the best men in Canada on our wheat board, men who have grown up in the selling of wheat. Last year we made a provision in our act whereby we would have two farmer members on that wheat board.
Some may ask as to the value of farm members on a grain selling agency. My answer is that the value of farmer members on a grain selling agency is that they are the only ones on that agency who have had experience as between the farmers and the elevators. I repeat they are the only ones who have had that experience-an experience which in my opinion is very necessary on the wheat board. We want qualified men of the very best calibre who will be in charge of taking wheat from the elevators and placing it in the hands of the consumers, wherever those consumers may be. But, in addition to that, we want our two farmer representatives on the wheat board who will be able to speak for the farmers in transactions between the wheat fields and the elevators. I would hope that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) would lose no time in placing the two farmer members on the board, so that it may operate on the advice of those farmers, and may carry out its duties in perhaps an even more perfect manner than it has done in past years.
The international wheat agreement will soon come up for renewal. I think every hon. member who is interested in it will insist that the international wheat price should conform more closely to what the price of wheat should be in this country. Taking everything into consideration, I believe we have the men who will be able to make that possible for the future.
I do not want to hear too many members in the House of Commons complain about subsidies to food producers, when they are available. As I said a while ago, it is the only balance we have. It is the only guarantee that prices will not become too low, or so low that no one will produce, and people will not be able to eat. That is what the subsidies do. They take the place of what we see in other lines of business, in that they guarantee stability. That is the only way it can be brought about, when the fluctuation in yield varies from perhaps 500 million bushels down to 100 million bushels.
The same observations apply to livestock, and to other commodities the farmers produce. In this I would include even chickens and eggs. If a floor price of 38 cents a dozen for 55704-32i
The Address-Mr. Studer eggs is too low, then I think we should consider placing that floor price at 42 cents or 44 cents, as advocated by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.
The same observations would apply to hogs. But perhaps in connection with hogs the situation is not quite as simple as that. When we have free trade in a commodity between the United States and Canada we must consider whether in that country they have a floor price and whether, if they have, their floor price is $26 or $24, as it is here. Are we going to close the market when their price does not compare with ours? Have they a floor price on hogs that is higher or lower than our price-or have they no floor price, at all? My understanding is that they have none, and neither do they have a floor price on eggs. So if our floor price is higher than their price, eggs will come to Canada-and the same would apply to hogs being sold in Canada. If we are going to have free trade, it will have to work both ways. So that the government has to consider what is proper in order to maintain the industry over a long period of time.
I give notice here and now that the days of cheap food at the expense of the farmer are gone. Those days are gone, and the people of Canada are going to pay the same price for food as they pay for other commodities they believe essential. I give further notice that if the people of this country-labour, or whoever it may be-are going to earn their living by working a five-day week, eight hours per day, that is what we are going to do. And when that day comes throughout agriculture, that day when we work the same hours, it means that the price of food will be higher.

I do not think there is any man that smart in the whole wide world. Yet the hon. member suggests that the government is prolonging sessions.
I listened to filibusters in the House of Commons, filibusters that denied the right of every hon. member to vote. I was not elected to come to Ottawa to listen to filibusters; I was elected to come to Ottawa to vote on issues; and if I do not vote right the people will take care of me at the next election. Filibusters are a negation of democracy, and our socialist friends are responsible for one of them. Then our other friends in the opposition were responsible for another one in connection with resale price maintenance-about which we have not heard very much since that time.
Then, there is another hon. member representing the wonderful constituency of Fraser Valley who, I think, was responsible or at least partly responsible for another filibuster. I have no intention of coming down to Ottawa to listen to filibusters of any group, because when there are filibusters it means they have a weak argument.
That is what I think about filibusters. Then, I wish to make another brief observation in connection with what has been said regarding extending the time of the House of Commons. I refer to what was said by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright). He was telling the people in Melfort about the T. and T. boys in the House of Commons,


the Tuesday to Thursday members, the members who live in eastern Canada; he was telling them how they leave the House of Commons on Thursday and come back the following Tuesday with the result that the government has to regulate its activities to conform with the operations or the negligence, we might call it, of these members. If that is the case, it certainly should be corrected, but after listening to what they have had to say during the sessions I have been here I do not believe it is the fault of the government or that any criticism should be directed at the government in regard to the delaying of any of the processes of this House of Commons. It has been said, and truthfully so, that the government opens the session but the opposition closes it. My criticism of them is that they never close it.
Perhaps I should tell Satan to get behind me, but I should like to refer to some discussion that has occurred in Saskatchewan as to the amount of taxation levied upon the people of Saskatchewan as compared with what is levied upon the people in other parts of the Dominion of Canada. It is claimed that the farmers of Saskatchewan are paying more income tax than any other group in Canada under the same circumstances. Taking the picture as a whole, that is most certainly not the case.
It has also been claimed that the dominion government is taking more out of Saskatchewan in the form of taxes than it is putting back in. No one has been able to substantiate that argument, although it is decried from the housetops. They say over and over again that the dominion government is taking more money from the people of Saskatchewan than it is putting back in. I have the figures here and I wish I had the opportunity of presenting them to every person in Saskatchewan.
To make a long story short, taking all the figures and summarizing them, it boils down to the fact that the population of Saskatchewan is 6 per cent of that of the Dominion of Canada and if all the taxes imposed by the dominion government are equalized it works out to 2 per cent of the taxation of Canada. The dominion government is paying to the people of Saskatchewan through the dominion-provincial agreement, through subsidies for vocational training and public health, through old age pensions and family allowances, through crop failure payments, through social welfare and other assistance, a total of $75 for every man, woman and child in the province, whereas it takes out by taxation only $35.
Their policy in Saskatchewan has been to try to make the people believe this. They are ready to accept that. You know, our

socialist friends are wonderful people at believing things that are not true. If they believed things that were true they would not be socialists, they would just be Liberals. The other day we heard the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) refer to the packers. This has been his pet theme ever since I have been in this house. He has been telling us about how they have squeezed the lifeblood out of the people. But lo and behold, the hon. member told us that recently he had gone to see some of the packers and that he did not think now what he had formerly thought. He told us that maybe it is the retailer who is taking too much profit, that the packer might be all right.
If the hon. member for Selkirk has thrown in the sponge in this battle for farmers' rights then I will take it up for him. I am ready to say that the packers are getting too much, that the retailers are getting too much. Everybody between the producer and the consumer is getting more money than the producer is getting. I am ready to take up the fight for the farmer if the hon. member for Selkirk has called it a day in that regard.
If the hon. member is ready to say something on behalf of these packers I would tell him that he had better hie himself out to Saskatchewan and have a little talk with the government out there. There is a co-operative packing plant for sale in Swift Current. If he wants to see all these packers put out of business he should tell the government in Saskatchewan to buy this plant. They are always ready to say how good they are when it comes to making money. They should buy this plant and then they can put the packers that the hon. member is complaining about out of business. There is a wonderful opportunity there and they should not miss it.

We have been told by the socialists that certain people have been misrepresenting things. There was quite an agitation in the House of Commons the other day during the debate on external affairs. I do not know anyone in the world who could follow the socialist policy as they
The Address-Mr. Studer have been bringing it down for the last fifteen years. They have been following a most tortuous road for the past fifteen years; in fact I have never seen a more crooked one in the Dominion of Canada.
Every time they come down here they have a different story. I would say that the hon. members have not been misrepresented at any time about whom they associate with, or with whom they conduct their operations. If they are the kind of people who are above reproach, why is it that the Conservative party is not open to reproach? You never hear anyone say that they are associated with communists. No one would say that, because their record proves that they are not associated with communists. They criticize the government as much as anyone does, and I think they should, but no one accuses them of being communists. What about the Social Credit party? They put up the same arguments, they contradict government policy, but no one accuses them of being communists. Why? Because their record proves that they are not communists.
But that is not the case with the socialists' record. The socialists' policy is not a Canadian policy. Socialism is an ism that was created beyond the confines of Canada. It is world-wide in scope. That is why they do not owe allegiance to any country, that is why they owe allegiance to world socialism. That is why they cannot adopt the attitude that we would like to see people adopt who are loyal in their feelings. As we see them here in Canada, they are committed to world revolution. No one can deny that.
You cannot say that a communist has to be a socialist, but you do have to say that before you can be a communist you have to be a socialist. They do not call it the union of communist socialist republics, they call it the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. The word "communist" is not in there. You cannot have one without the other. Naturally they are committed to a world movement and a loyalty to countries does not prevent them from adopting the world attitude. I say to every hon. member of this House of Commons that it is indeed unfortunate that they have followers they do have, because no sooner does the leader of the socialists in this House of Commons make a speech in Massachusetts last week than we see on the very same day the leader of the Labour-Progressive party, of which this house has heard so much, making a statement in Saskatchewan where the Labour-Progressive communist party is meeting. The other day we listened to a fine speech on immigration delivered by the member for Spadina (Mr. Croll). It outlined the need of a country such as ours for people from other lands who would join with us to make our country greater. We need people of British stock, people from Scotland, France, Ireland, central Europe and United States, in fact any people who are willing to adopt our policies. I was impressed also by the speech of the hon. member who warned us to be cautious and not reckless in connection with immigration. I think we should have these people, but the best Canadians are right here in Canada. If we get stock from these other countries, then I want to say that the real purebred stock is right here in Canada, our own boys and girls that are growing up here. These are the people who have a future in Canada. The fathers and mothers of these

children believe the children should be part and parcel of the good things that Canada holds in the future for all its people. We should join with these immigrants who come to Canada in an effort to make this Canada of ours great.
I should like, therefore, to pay a tribute to the fathers and mothers of this country who are raising our young Canadians, perhaps under great difficulties. We welcome those who may come from other countries, and we join hands with them and with those who live here, so that coming generations will work for the welfare of a happier Canada.

speechtext:
I am
afraid, Mr. Speaker, that I cannot be a dynamic orator such as the one to whom we have just listened. I like to hear him speak because he can say more in ten minutes than most of us can say in twenty-five. I agree with some of the things he has said, especially the tribute he paid to the Irish. A year and a half ago I paid them a similar tribute in this house, making special mention of their virility, which is largely due to the eating of potatoes. I showed that these people had an interest in our province, and if we could get more of them into it we would be very happy because the consumption of potatoes is not what it should be. If it were not for the Irishmen we could not grow potatoes at all.
There are some things in connection with the hon. member's speech with which I should like to deal, especially his reference to redistribution, but there will be an opportunity for that later. I do not think the hon. member had the right point of view when referring to that famous province, the province of Prince Edward Island. I know that before the redistribution bill leaves this house the hon. member will fully understand what it means to Canada to have four representatives from Prince Edward Island in this house.
Before going on with what I wish to say I should like to refer, in a different spirit, to the passing of our late King George VI, a great monarch who bequeathed to the people of this country a great prestige. While his reign was not as long as some others it stands as a greater monument to democracy than that of any other monarch in the world. We mourn his passing. Now, for the sixth time in the history of England, we find a queen coming to the throne in her own right. People across the world have joined in proclaiming Princess Elizabeth Alexandra Mary as Queen Elizabeth II by the grace of God; and at this time I say "Long live the queen".
The Address-Mr. McLure
I have a few things to say. I shall be as brief as possible, but I offer no apology for taking part in this debate at this time. The debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne gives members of this house an opportunity to present in one form or another the problems of their constituencies. The address read by His Excellency is the program of the government, and it is our duty as members to examine that program for its omissions and commissions. Before dealing with that, however, I want to offer a few congratulations. In the first place I congratulate two young men from Prince Edward Island, Mr. Allan MacDonald, a Scotsman, and Mr. Walter Reid, an Irishman. These students from St. Dunstan's university have won the debating championship of the whole of Canada, according to press reports; and their final score was made right here in the federal capital of Canada about ten days ago. I also want to congratulate the farmers of my constituency and my province. Again according to the press Prince Edward Island has won the reputation of having the best hogs for bacon to be found anywhere in the world, and last year we led every province in Canada in our percentage of first quality animals. Also within the last two weeks or so an exhibition has been going on down in Florida, and Prince Edward Island seed potatoes have topped all others as the only ones absolutely free of disease. That is something very worth while because if you do not have the best seed you cannot grow good potatoes.
I am not going to forget my congratulations to the mover (Mr. George) and seconder (Mr. Gauthier, Lake St. John) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They did honour to their constituencies as well as to themselves. I know the mover; he is a maritimer, and when it was learned that he was to open this debate you could hear it said around the corridors, "Let George do it!" Well, George did it and did it well.
In criticizing this speech we do not criticize the mover or seconder, because after all it is only the program of the government and as I said a moment ago we have a perfect right to criticize that speech as we see fit. After you go over that speech and read it carefully, and after you listen to the debate for and against in this house, you see that it is a very ordinary speech. Since this debate commenced some excellent speeches have been made. I was glad to be here to listen to my leader, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), because he made a wonderful speech. He was followed by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) who also

The Address

Mr. McLure made an excellent speech. As we have followed the debate we have heard other men acquit themselves well.
I am not going to take up the political side of this question; I am going to refer more to my own constituency. That is what is of interest to me, and I hope I can make it of some interest to the government, though I am sorry there are no government leaders in the front row opposite. They have done many things for which they might deserve some praise; but in speaking of my province I have to do so from the point of view of how this government has dealt with us. I have to be like the soldier who was asked why he scratched himself, and replied, "I always scratch where it itches the most." From time to time in this 'house I have spoken on one subject in particular, the subject that means the most to us; that is transportation, which is creating a great deal of talk in our province right now.
In connection with this matter of transportation the government of the day, like most governments we have had, have neglected our province. I have suggested this before, and again I charge them with wilful neglect, with not doing justice to Prince Edward Island under the terms of the union. I am not unmindful of the demands we have made on the government. Since I came here in 1945 I am not unmindful of getting after the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) with regard to the new steamer for us. Finally, after a couple of years of goading, we secured an excellent boat, the Abegweit, to replace the
5.5.	Charlottetown which was lost. The
5.5.	Charlottetown was lost while on her way from Borden to Saint John, N.B. for repairs. Had the government of the day fulfilled the terms and the recommendations of the Andrew Rae Duncan commission of 1926 and had fulfilled the terms of union of 1873, we would not have lost the S.S. Charlottetown because she would have been repaired in the province in Which she was in service. Recommendations were made by the Andrew Rae Duncan commission for the improvement of the harbour situation of Charlottetown and for building what was to be called a drydock or, as it is called today, a marine railway slip. This was a promise that was given to us by the government, but it is one that they have never even tried to fulfil.
I want to say just a few words further with reference to transportation. To my surprise I find that the Canadian maritime commission, authorized by this government, has now the full authority over all our transportation problems. They say yes or no, and with respect to our problem of transportation they do not seem to know anything but no. Let

us look for a moment at the last decision or so that they have given. We in the maritimes know, as do most of the members of this house, that we have two ferry systems. One is called the Borden-Tormentine ferry system, with two ships, namely the Abegweit and the Prince Edward. This Borden-Tormentine ferry is doing an excellent job for us. This ferry was given to us by the Borden government as part of the fulfilment of the terms of union of 1873. Besides the Borden-Tormentine ferry, we have another ferry operated by Northumberland Ferries Limited, giving service between Wood Island and Caribou. This ferry is a little different from the other one.
The Borden-Tormentine ferry is a government ferry, a government service, while the Northumberland ferry system is a private enterprise ferry subsidized by the dominion government. This ferry, known as the Wood Island-Caribou ferry-operated, as I said a moment ago, by the Northumberland Ferries Limited-has given an efficient service to farmers, fishermen and others. As a matter of fact, during the last two years the traffic on this ferry has become so great that it is impossible for the company to handle it. I might say further that this company has done a great deal in the interests of farmers, fishermen and the tourist industry. It is, however, a common thing to go down to this ferry, either on the Wood Island side or on the Nova Scotia side, and to find there long queues of cars and trucks waiting for transportation, notwithstanding the fact that they have two boats. One of them is small and one of them is fairly large. They are the Prince Nova and the Charles A. Dunning; but they cannot handle the traffic at all, especially in the months of June, July and August. This company has submitted facts and figures to the government. I am not going to put on record, as I did before, the figures showing growth of traffic over this ferry, because, within the last ten days, the government has had the facts and figures placed before them; they have been placed before the maritime commission and, through that commission, before the Department of Transport, with all the details to which consideration should have been given. The commission listened to the delegation that came here and spent three or four days. I was not on that delegation nor was I even invited in on it; but I learned that they did not have a good reception given to them by the Canadian maritime commission.
The commission accepted their briefs in order to stow them away, but the decision they came to, when the briefs were presented

and they were asked to assist in getting a new boat of larger dimensions for this Wood Islandi-Caribou ferry, without even going over the briefs, was "nothing doing"; and they never gave a legitimate reason for it. You could not, however, expect anything else from this commission. In the first place, I do not believe there was one man on that commission who knew the terms of confederation of 1873 or the recommendations with regard to transportation contained in the report of the Andrew Rae Duncan commission of 1926. For a commission of that kind to veto the proposals of this delegation, to the detriment of traffic from Wood Island to Caribou, is something that I think should be fully considered. I might say this. In my humble opinion the delegation made a mistake twice over. The first one was this. When this commission told them "nothing doing", right there and then they should have stated: We will not accept your decision in any form. The other mistake they made was this. They should never have gone before this commission, notwithstanding the fact that it may have been appointed in some way by the government. On transportation questions we are not dealing with subcontractors-although sometimes we have been subjected to them-but we must deal directly with the Minister of Transport and the government. If we were dealing with them, we could turn around, and say:	Here
is our proposition; you owe this province of Prince Edward Island1 proper transportation according to the terms of confederation. Give this to us at the present time. One little excuse was made about three months ago that there was a shortage of steel. When the delegates come back again they will have another excuse about the economy of the country. And yet they want our people to become producers. After they become producers of foodstuffs they will not give them the proper means of transporting their produce to market. I mention this to show that the commission, had no right and no knowledge to study a problem of that kind.
I wish to say on behalf of the Wood Island ferry that during the railway strike of two years ago it was the only connecting link, in so far as transportation is concerned, between our province and the mainland. During that time the ferry gave a wonderful service. I might carry this question a little further. I hope that hon. members will not look at this question as if we were trying to get something for nothing. This company was willing to pay its share of building the boat. They were willing to enter into a contract over a period of years. Even when they were
The Address-Mr. McLure shut off and it was said that there was nothing doing for them they went to the United States and found that they could get four or five boats there that, with a little alteration, would have given good service in the Northumberland ferry service. But an order in council was passed which said that no Canadian could buy boats for the next five or six years. Therefore that proposition was vetoed. I hope that our legislature in Prince Edward Island, which is sitting at the present time, will not accept the refusal of this commission. I hope-I am going to guess right on this-that they will bring a new petition before the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier) and the government and that they will succeed in getting what they truly deserve.
I have a few more things with reference to my constituency that I might mention. While they may not be of direct interest to other hon. members, that does not bother me. They still are of interest to me as one of the representatives of Queens constituency. In our province we had two elections recently. Going back to 1945 I find that a great number of promises were made by the Liberal party. First of all, in 1945 we had the promise that a fine dominion building would be erected in Charlottetown. It was a good promise for an election, but we heard nothing more of it until we commenced asking questions on the floor of the house; and even up until the other day nobody seemed to know anything about this building at Charlottetown.
They told us repeatedly that it would be built. They even bought some properties on which the building is to be erected. In addition to that, they drew extensive plans and they even made cuts of the building and had them published before the election by all the press of the island, saying: Here is this wonderful building. When I ask the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) when it is to be built I find that he does not know. I suppose it will be held out as another promise to be made use of in the next election. We will have to wait for that.
For the last five years we have also been promised-and the records of the house will show that-a naval barracks. In answer to a question of mine last year the minister told us that the naval barracks would be built. We have had that promise ever since 1946. The same thing is true of the armouries.
The armouries building was promised definitely three years ago, but we are farther away from it now that we were then, because the last excuse was that there was one other place promised one first, and when it was

The Address-Mr. McLure built then we might have ours next. I understand that they are not going to build the other one for the next four or five years, but we are still playing second fiddle.
Another thing we were promised definitely was harbour improvements and marine railway slips. I have brought this matter up on several occasions. Every government and every party are committed to these two particular promises. These things are badly needed in our province, but nothing has been done so far with regard to them.
I shall leave the public building for the time being. In reading over the speech from the throne I was disappointed to find no mention of incapacitated people. I had hoped, as many others had, that in the speech from the throne we would find that that part of the social security plan would come into effect at this time. The only thing I see is that in the notices of motions on the order paper motion No. 10 which reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of co-operating with the provincial governments for the purpose of providing pensions, equal to old age pensions, for all those who are incapacitated and unable to earn their living, regardless of age.
I find that motion No. 22 on today's order paper is along the same lines. If we ever reach these notices of motions I am sure the house will take a deep interest in the discussion, as it should. Only today I received a letter which is so pitiable that I hate to put it on the record. It has to do with a family of three who are incapacitated. They are receiving a little money. From the local government they get $10 a month, and from the civic government of Charlottetown they get $10 a month. They have to pay $12 a month rent, and all they have to live on is $8. Only one of the three is able to walk. The other two, on account of the dread disease of polio, are completely incapacitated. Although I have nothing to say against the action of the government in connection with the social security measures they have brought forward, I say it should have done something for these incapacitated people. I believe it is on record that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) made what amounted almost to a definite promise that this year provision would be made in the speech from the throne whereby these unfortunate people would be cared for.
Then I would turn to another matter connected with pensions. In common with many other hon. members, I have referred to pensions paid to those who have retired under the old pension plan. Before the increased cost of living, the amount they received was almost sufficient for their purposes. Today


however it is quite inadequate. I am thinking particularly of those who worked for the railways, as well as others who held civil service positions.
Many of those pensioners retired on amounts as low as $25 a month. But even those who are receiving $90 or $100 today are not receiving sufficient to live on. This is also true, and even more unfortunate, in respect of widows in receipt of pensions. There was some inkling in the speech from the throne that action would be taken. Before I left my home to come to Ottawa I had visited a number of these pensioners. I have in mind one man who had worked 43 years, having entered the service at an early age. Upon his retirement two years ago he felt that, after working that length of time, he would have enough pension on which to live. He found however that he had to sell his property and then look for a job. This man had a family to support.
Because of the small pension he received, he had to come again into the labour market. However, if the government had increased his pension as it should have been increased, to a point where it would take care of the increased cost of living, he would not have had to re-enter the labour market and thus take a job from someone else.
There were other matters I had intended at this time to bring to the attention of the house but, as the time at my disposal is almost exhausted, I shall terminate what I had intended to say. In closing I would repeat what I said earlier with respect to transportation, and I would hope that other hon. members would take up the cause of the incapacitated people in all districts of Canada. To them more than to any other class we owe a livelihood, in this fair country of ours.
Prince Edward Island is certainly one province that has done and is doing its full share in the production of foodstuffs for both the domestic and export markets. As I said earlier, however, if we do not have proper transportation facilities our people will find it difficult to produce, only to find that it cannot be transported to the point of consumption. I had intended to make some further observations, among which were some references to the postal service in Prince Edward Island, but I shall defer those remarks until a later time.
