But with all the qualities he does possess, I think hon. members will agree with me that sometimes those who are politically mature get erroneous interpretations, come to wrong conclusions and give bad judgments. These are the words of the hon. member, as they are reported in Hansard:
I think he was very ill-advised in making that sort of speech, particularly in trying to tie us in with the communist party.
Those who followed what I had to say, or read in Hansard what I said, will certainly not be able to come to that conclusion. I certainly agree with this observation of the hon. member:
I should like to remind the hon. member that he agrees with old age pensions. So do the L.P.P. and Tim Buck; they openly proclaimed that fact. The hon. member agrees with unemployment insurance, and so does Tim Buck. The hon. member agrees on family allowances and all those social security measures. When the government proposes such measures, and the hon. member supports them in this house, then Tim Buck states in the Tribune that he agrees with all those social security measures and has been fighting for them for years, does the hon. member believe that places him and the members of this house in the communist camp?
Of course I agree with that statement; but he has missed the point completely. I believe he has deliberately missed the point, because if he had examined my speech more closely he would have noted that I tried to stress the following statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), which I read into my speech the other day:
The real danger as I see it, and as I pointed out in my broadcast on Tuesday night, is that the policy of his party-
He was referring to the leader of the C.C.F. party.
-as it was stated in that council declaration, will play straight into the hands of communist propaganda.
I went out of my way to be most careful in what I said, and if the hon. member will
The Address-Mr. Decore refer again to the report of my speech at page 462 of Hansard he will find that after making that quotation I said:
In quoting from this communist paper may I first of all make it clear that, in so far as the leader of the C.C.F. party is concerned. I have a lot of respect for him. I have here a short Canadian Press report dated Toronto, March 7, which is symptomatic of a considerable number of such reports. It reads:


Shocked by Lack of Religious Note at Ottawa Service
A resolution unanimously passed by the Toronto diocesan board of the Church of England said a "multitude of Canadians" were "inexpressibly shocked" by "lack of any religious ceremony" at the national memorial service in Ottawa on the day of the king's funeral.
This is a Christian country, and surely it would have been appropriate that something of a religious nature such as a prayer, for example, should have been included in such a ceremony. In fact a ceremony of that kind by its very nature is religious; it must be. Every day we open the proceedings of this assembly with prayers, and I think that meets with universal approval on the part of the members and the people of this country. That being so, why should a ceremony of so much greater national significance, such as the memorial service for our late king, which was also broadcast, contain nothing at all of a religious nature? It is very difficult for me to understand why it was done in that way. Certainly the local ceremonies held across the country were not characterized by that sort of action. The one held in my own city of Calgary was very different. There a large meeting was held in the arena, attended by I have forgotten how many thousands of people. Mr. Speaker, before the dinner recess I had dealt with two or three subjects-commendably briefly I hope-and I have two or three more upon which I wish to comment, also briefly, at the present time.
First of all, I should like to say something about what I can only call the blast delivered by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) to the automobile dealers association. In my opinion, this was nothing more than a red herring to divert public attention away from the fact that automobile prices in this country are much higher than they are in the United States, almost entirely owing to the fact that we have such excessively high sales

The Address-Mr. Harkness
tax, excise tax and customs duties applied against these necessary means of moving about.
I should like to make it quite clear that I am not speaking as an advocate of the automobile dealers association but rather on behalf of the consumer who is the man who has to pay for cars these extremely high prices which have removed from the average man the possibility of securing a car; and this is a development which I at least think is a bad one as far as this country is concerned.
One of the things which distinguished this continent from the Rio Grande north, at any rate, from the countries of Europe and from other parts of the world was the fact that the ordinary worker, the ordinary man, the man with an average income, could buy an automobile, an electric refrigerator probably, and these other things, which to a large number of people at least make life desirable and to some extent worth living. The fact that our average man, our average worker, could secure these things distinguished him-and made a big difference in his outlook-from his counterpart in the countries of Europe. The fact that the prices of automobiles and, to some extent, those of other appliances have now become so high, largely owing to government taxation, is, I think, going to store up for us in the future a great deal of trouble in the matter of what has often been referred to as class warfare, class distinction and things of that sort. That is the type of development which, from every point of view, it is in our interest to put an end to.
Hon. members of this house may recall that I have spoken on this subject here before; in fact, I did so long before the automobile dealers started their present campaign. I therefore do not think that the accusation can be made against me that any remarks I make on this subject have been prompted by that campaign or by them. The last occasion on which I spoke on the matter was in the throne speech debate of last session. On October 15, as reported at page 61 of Hansard of that date, I said, among other things, this which I should like to repeat:
Let me take one example in the manufacturing line,-
This is of high prices.
-because so far as manufactured goods in Canada are concerned we find a situation anything but reasonable. Nearly all manufactured goods are priced considerably higher than in the United States; there is no question about it. Let us look at automobile prices. A two-door model of a well-known so-called low-priced automobile, one of the best known on this continent, sells in New York for $1,598, while in Ottawa, from information supplied by the dealers, it sells for $2,335. Why do we see this difference of $737?
Since that time I have taken the trouble to secure some more prices and the tax figures when applied to those particular models of automobiles, and there is one more that I should like to put on the record. It is the case of a Chevrolet automobile, one of the lower-priced models. The price before taxes in the United States-and this is without freight costs added; it is really in the factory towns, you might say-is $1,473.50. The price in Canada, under similar circumstances, is $1,757.06. That is a difference of $283.56. The price is $283.56 cheaper in the United States than in Canada. The federal excise and sales taxes in the United States are $120. In Canada they are $473.94, a difference of $353.94. The Canadian purchaser has to pay $353.94 more than his counterpart in the United States. If you add up those figures you will find that the total price to the consumer is as follows: In the United States $1,593.50; in Canada, $2,231, a difference of $637.50. In this country these people in the same circumstances, buying a so-called low-priced car, are forced to pay $637.50 more. The difference in price of $353.94, due to excise and sales taxes alone, is of course entirely due to the policy that this government has followed in taxing matters with regard to automobiles and, of course, other appliances, particularly electrical appliances of all sorts. The further difference of $283.56 is due to customs duties.
As far as I can see, there is no essential reason why the cost of manufacturing a car in Canada should be that much greater than it is in the United States. The wages are lower in our industry in Canada. The general factory costs are lower, including factory sites, the building of the factory and all that sort of thing. It is true that a certain number of parts are imported from the United States, and therefore they probably cost more. But certainly I can see no reason for this large difference of $283.56. There is no question that most of this is due to the fact, not that the cost of manufacturing cars is that much greater in Canada but that the customs duties make it possible for the manufacturer to sell the car for that much more, without taxes, than does his counterpart in the United States.
The need for an automobile by large numbers of Canadians does not require argument, I think; it is self-apparent. To practically all farmers at the present time an automobile is essential. To a large number of craftsmen, factory workers and manual workers of all sorts, an automobile is also essential in order that they may get to their places of employment. This is all to say

The Address-Mr. Harkness nothing of large numbers of people in businesses of all kinds for whom an automobile is a necessity. In western Canada, because the distances, comparatively, between any places of population-whether it be villages, towns or cities-are much greater than they are in the central provinces, this need for an automobile in the west is really much greater than it is in the central provinces. Unfortunately our prices are higher there than in the central provinces because of very high freight costs. At the present time the cost of shipping a car from the factory here in Ontario to Alberta runs between $250 and $300. So that even some of the people on comparative salaries or wages who could buy a car here find it impossible to buy one in Alberta because of that difference in freight.
The prices of cars can be brought down very drastically by the action of this government, and really only by that means. That is the only way in which they can be brought down. There are two ways in which they can be brought down. The first is by lowering the excessively high sales and excise taxes; and second, by reducing the protection of Canadian manufacturers, through lowering the customs duty, to the point where they have only the protection they require to keep in operation, which I am sure is very small.
In leaving this particular matter I will only say that I sincerely hope the Minister of Finance, when he produces his budget in about three weeks' time, will include provisions in the budget along these lines, giving some relief to people so far as the price not only of automobiles but of other manufactured appliances of various kinds is concerned. It is all very well to talk about the comparative cost of living in this country and in the United States. None of these things is really included in the cost of living index, and therefore it does not by any means represent what the real cost is to a very large number of people of holding a job and carrying on their business, particularly if it is a farming business, and so on. The difference in price of these things between United States and Canada alone makes the differential against us very serious. One of the reasons why I may perhaps harp on the subject is that I think it is one of the reasons our people leave this country and go to the United States. It is one of the reasons why we lose native-born and educated population to the United States. They can readily find out what the prices are of things like automobiles, and many of our young people say: Why should I not go down there, get a job and buy these things more cheaply? Therefore from that point of view, as well as from the general

economic point of view, it would be very much in our interest if the prices of these things in the United States and in Canada could be brought much closer together.
There is one other tax which the Minister of Finance mentioned, and on which I should like to say a word, namely, the tax on cigarettes. I think it is admitted now by everybody, including the minister, probably, that that tax has reached the point where diminishing returns are being received. That alone is sufficient to condemn it. From the bare return point of view alone it is a bad tax, because it is producing less returns than it produced before it was increased. In addition to that, of course, there is the thing which has received a great deal of publicity, namely, the amount of smuggling which this tax has encouraged. From these two points of view alone it would be to the advantage of the country to get some reduction in the cigarette tax.
I turn to the last subject upon which I have anything to say, Mr. Speaker, namely, the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease. In my opinion this is the most calamitous event which has occurred in Canada for a long time. The loss of the United States market will cripple our livestock industry very seriously for as long as that market is closed to us, apart from the loss we may have through animals being destroyed, or anything else along that line. However, in addition to the current loss of the United States market, which is bound to continue for some time under the best of circumstances, we have in operation in this country a series of provincial embargoes which have completely disrupted the normal marketing of livestock in our own country. These embargoes are rapidly producing some areas where there is a serious shortage of meat, and other areas where there is a very serious over-supply of livestock of all kinds and meat. As a matter of fact, the situation in which they are now is that there are no markets available to the producers at all, practically speaking. That is a situation which, for the protection of both the producer and the consumer, should be rectified just as rapidly as it is possible to do so.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) was urged in this chamber and in other quarters to call a conference of the provincial authorities with himself in order that a settlement of the present extremely unsatisfactory conditions might be worked out. I have heard nothing since the discussion we had on this matter was concluded in the house, about this conference having been arranged. The minister went out to Regina, returned here last week and said that on his

trip out west he had talked with the Saskatchewan and Manitoba authorities and by telephone with the British Columbia authorities. Such means as that are not, I think, likely to be as effective as getting representatives of all the governments together, and with them all together working out a solution of this problem. I do not think there is any question that a solution satisfactory to all concerned could be worked out. It is merely a matter of getting them to see each other's point of view and getting the thing done. I think that a conference of all the people concerned is probably the most likely way of getting that accomplished. As a result, I would hope that the minister would convene this conference without any further delay and try to get on with the matter.
My own province, from the producer's point of view, is probably the worst off of any. We just have not markets, for we have no place where we can go with our livestock. We cannot go to British Columbia; we cannot come east. All we have is the local market which, in comparison with the amount of livestock produced in Alberta, is extremely small, Fortunately, people have been holding their livestock off the market to a very large extent, waiting for some settlement, you might say, of this provincial embargo matter to be made. A lot of people are not going to be able to do that indefinitely for various reasons. As far as some livestock are concerned, lambs and hogs, there is only a certain length of time that you can hold them off the market. If you hold them longer the value decreases very greatly.
Perhaps the provinces with embargoes in effect are unwilling to remove them because of lack of confidence in the means which has been taken up to date to restrict the disease to the area in which it broke out. That point of view may have validity. I think that more could have been done and should be done immediately to ensure that this disease does not spread beyond its borders.
My information from a very reliable source in that quarantined area is that the quarantine is not as effective as one would hope. For example, the people in the area are still moving about quite freely. They go into the towns, into the city of Regina, which is included in the area. They mix with other people, and without any special disinfection of their clothing and so forth taking place, without really anything having been done along that line, to prevent the spread of the disease, unless the conscientious farmer himself may have done it more or less on his own initiative. I understand the only means of enforcing the quarantine in that whole area

The most serious thing, however, that has been revealed to me, so far as the foot-and-mouth disease is concerned, is that considerable numbers of deer have been seen moving about in the quarantined area. My own view is that these deer constitute perhaps the greatest threat of all of the disease spreading right across Canada. There are a considerable number of deer in the Qu'Appelle river valley, which is part of the quarantined area. From that river valley the deer can readily travel both east and west, and into all the other river valleys right across the country.
It seems to me that if this disease is to be confined to its present area, then one of the most essential things to be done is to put an end to the danger of spreading the infection through these deer.
I was told by a man who had been in the area for ten days that he had seen five deer jumping over a fence from the fields of one of the farms where the cattle had been infected, and by that time slaughtered. On another occasion there were more than twenty deer counted along the banks of Was-cana creek, which the Minister of Agriculture said in the house was in his opinion the source of infection. At the moment, Mr. Speaker, my constituents are faced with a serious problem which affects their economy and the economy of Canada. That is the epidemic of foot-and-mouth disease which recently developed in several municipalities around Regina and in an abattoir in that city. The manner in which the disease was brought to the attention of the provincial and federal authorities is common knowledge. The steps taken to make the diagnosis and limit the spread of the disease are also well known. The success with which these efforts have been crowned is becoming increasingly clear. There has been no extension of the disease beyond the quarantine area within which there is a cattle population of 25,000 under close farm to farm observation.
I have but recently returned from Regina, where I found complete satisfaction on the part of the authorities and the people with the manner in which the epidemic was being handled. They were resentful of the undue publicity given this disaster in this house, which caused the other provinces to think the disease was much more severe and much more widespread than actually was the case, and which implied laxity and inefficiency on the part of those men in the federal health of animals division who are dealing with the epidemic. They feel this type of criticism will create the impression abroad that the epidemic is not being properly dealt with and the quarantine is not being rigidly observed, and that as a consequence the ruinous embargo will be unduly prolonged. Some hon. members will remember the depression and drought years that we endured in Saskatchewan. Our grain planted in the spring did not germinate. The grass did not grow. Our fields became black. Our cattle wandered from one blade of grass to another, from one pothole to another seeking water, until they were starving and had to be shot. Then we were given the magnificent sum of $15 per head.

Mr. Speaker, I feel that there has been too much heat and perhaps not quite enough light generated in this debate. From here on let us proceed calmly. Let us leave it to the committee on agriculture to hear these people before they are condemned, to decide if there is any fault, and to place the blame where it belongs. As for the rest of us, we can ill afford to make capital out of a calamity of this magnitude. Let us try to work together to restore the confidence of the people, in and outside of Canada, so that we can have this embargo removed as soon as possible.
I want to say a word about a man who has stuck his nose into this matter; I refer to Mr. Alvin- Hamilton, the Progressive Conservative leader in Saskatchewan, the man who is going to lose his deposit in the forthcoming election.

I am just talking about Saskatchewan. I want to tell you that in this house last week a statement was made by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), that in December it was common knowledge among the farmers of Saskatchewan whose herds were affected that this malady was foot-and-mouth disease, that everybody was talking about it. I presume -that was the information that was given to him by Mr. Hamilton when Mr. Hamilton briefed him, and before he made this statement in the house. Then, on a broadcast a few days later Mr. Hamilton, when asked a question by one of the reporters,-do you

believe that statement is true? he said no. He said: I was canvassing in that district. You know, he is a candidate in Lumsden, where this disease is. "I was canvassing in this district throughout January and February", he said on the radio, "and I did not know that the disease existed until I read it in the press". Gentlemen, he is canvassing in that district. Mr. Thayer, one of the C.C.F., is a provincial member in that constituency. My brother farms in that constituency. Regina adjoins the constituency. The constituency of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) adjoins it. The people including the above-named were unaware of it; they thought they were quite safe. They thought it was vesicular stomatitis.
There is another matter that I should like to bring up tonight, which affects the members of my constituency. I want the members of the C.C.F. party to hang onto their seats when they hear this. I hold in my hand letters from many unions in my municipality. There was a general impression that mail from unions all went to a certain part of the house, but I received some, which is closely related to the matter that I have to deal with. I refer to the plight of some of my constituents who are employed in the packing houses, and to some of the Canadian brotherhood of railway employees. I have representations here from the queen of the west, division 43, the Canadian brotherhood of railway employees; from the united packing houses of America, local 226; united packing houses of America, local 373; retail and wholesale department stores union, local 538. May I point out that on account of the federally placed quarantine these men will be more severely injured; they will face greater hardship than similar unions in other parts of Canada. For example, starting in the mari-times, Quebec, Ontario, Manitoba and British Columbia have placed provincial embargoes. Therefore the workers in these areas can hold the provincial authorities responsible. The federal authorities did not put them on, and the federal authorities wish to have these embargoes removed immediately. In Regina it is a different matter. We are quarantined in an area fifty miles square. No produce can move in or out. These railway men are completely out of employment. Some consideration should be given to this matter. It applies also to the same extent to the packing 'house workers. I ask the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) to look into the needs of these men and give them that charitable consideration for which he is gaining such an enviable reputation.
The Address-Mr. McCusker
There is one other matter which has to do with the truckers. I have been receiving many letters from them. I have dozens of letters from them. I understand that their case is being considered by the board of transport commissioners, and it is therefore not proper for me to discuss it at this time.
One other matter that I should like to deal with before I sit down is housing. At present we are trying to make arrangements with the federal government to build 150 houses in Regina on the basis of the federal government putting up 75 per cent, the province 12i per cent and the city 12-J per cent. This will not begin to meet our needs. At the present time we have a waiting list in Regina of 1,500 veterans families who require houses. We have people employed in Regina who cannot find homes. We had two employed in a firm in Regina in which I am interested. They had to leave. One of them came back to Toronto and the other went to Battleford because they could not find accommodation in which to house their families. Arrangements were made so that loans could be placed with four insurance companies, but these loans are for a type of house that is too expensive for the young people starting in life to build. The chamber of commerce has put forth some reasons why assistance should be given to private citizens to build houses. They list the advantages. They consist of more variety and attractiveness in design because of individual choice; pride of ownership and care of property; more personal supervision in construction; many contractors employed instead of one large contractor.
In the old days, before we had subsidized housing and gave the entire contract to one large firm, there were many small contractors. One or two carpenters and a plasterer formed a little firm and hired a few men. They worked long hours. They built better houses. The prospective owner was there in the morning and in the evening filling in and assisting. He got a better and a cheaper house. That is a thing of the past.
Another advantage is the dispersal of homes throughout the city instead of grouping them into districts. They ask for the restoration of the additional loan of one-sixth. They want to make it possible to grant loans on modest houses, modern or non-modern. When the city of Regina was built years ago, and when I first started to work, we did not have modem houses. Gradually this has changed, but the construction of those days was not destroyed; it was improved upon. We cannot subsidize a man to build a small modern house with two bedrooms, or one bedroom, sitting room and kitchen. No, it must have

The Address-Mr. J. J. Smith three bedrooms. Young people just starting out in life cannot afford that. The question often asked is: What if he has a family? My answer to that is: When a family comes along he will have established himself and will be able to afford a better house. He will be able to sell the one he is in now to some other young people just getting married and starting out in life. I ask the minister to give some attention to these people who are in considerable difficulty at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, in taking part in this debate there are a few things that I wish to call to the attention of the government; but before doing that there is another matter with which I should like to deal for a few minutes. It has to do with what took place in this chamber on Friday evening. I assure hon. members that I am not going to deal with external affairs. I will do as I have always done in this house, namely, speak about something that I am familiar with. However, my colleague, the hon. member for Humboldt (Mr. Hetland), brought a subject before the house that I think was timely. It was high time that the matter was mentioned.
I have nothing to add to what the hon. member had to say other than to remark that the two hon. members from the C.C.F. party who criticized him for what he did were unfair; their remarks were unwarranted. Of course my friend the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) could possibly be excused because he does not know the conditions of the farmers in western Canada. For that reason we will excuse him. It is possible that he did not gather the motive of the hon. member for Humboldt, and, as I say, he can be excused, but there is no excuse for the attack of the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight), and the references he made to the hon. member for Humboldt. Possibly he and his colleagues in that party, along with other hon. members, will agree with me before I am through that that was unfair and uncalled for.
I should be fair to the hon. member for Cape Breton South. He did pay what is, in my opinion, a compliment to the hon. member for Humboldt when he said that the hon. member was politically immature. Well, I do not know the people in the Humboldt constituency, but I presume they are much the same as the electors in my constituency. I would presume, too, that they would want their member to remain politically immature. So long as he is practically political, that is good enough. And if I am here three or four years, or nine or ten, when anyone rises in his place and says that I am politically immature I will accept it as a compliment.


What was the hon. member for Humboldt putting before the house? As I recall it he said that on many occasions when unions strike they did not strike against their employers, but against every man, woman and child in Canada. If I were to criticize the remarks of the hon. member for Humboldt I would say that he was much too kind. I think he could have added, when he was referring to the railway strike, that that strike was against the farmers of western Canada, and that it affected them to a greater degree than any other class of people in this country. I believe all members, regardless of their political complexion, from the prairie provinces will agree with me when I make that statement. And I will go further and say that the farmers from the prairies are still suffering from the effects of that strike.
I am quite satisfied that I will not be contradicted when I make these statements. That being so, I would suggest that any hon. member referring to the remarks of the hon. member for Humboldt, while speaking in this debate, either refrain from speaking or compliment the -hon. member for Humboldt for bringing the matter to the attention of the house.
On Friday, March 14, as reported at page 474 of Hansard, the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight), referring to the hon. member for Humboldt, had this to say:
I cannot understand the bitter attack against the working people of this country by the hon. member for Humboldt

Well, there was nothing bitter in his attack. I do not know what the motive of the hon. member for Saskatoon might have been, but I suggest that if he is going to try to convince the people in Saskatchewan that the little gentleman from Humboldt is bitter, either in this house or out of it, then he had better save his breath to cool his porridge.
As was pointed out by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher), I think those of us from Saskatchewan, as well as those from Alberta and other constituencies on the prairies, would be well advised to co-operate in our problems, and not to get into political fights in the house. It is true that we are likely this summer to have an election in Saskatchewan. After all, those of us who want a good political scrap will find nothing to stop us from getting out in Saskatchewan and doing it right there. But I do resent it when any member from the prairie provinces accuses a supporter of the government of making a bitter attack, and proceeds to censure him when, in fact, the bon. member in question is simply trying to put a case clearly

before the house. He is told, in effect: You keep quiet, or we will slap you down. I cannot stand for that.
I believe that since I have come here I have tried at all times to reach logical conclusions which would be for the benefit of all. I believe hon. members in the opposition would agree that I have tried to do that. I say this, not as a threat, but as a warning that if the opposition wish to turn this honourable house into a rough-house, then we boys from Saskatchewan will accommodate them. I say this to the government leader in the house and to the whips, that if they think they can stop us, then they are badly mistaken, because we will not be tramped on.
I shall now turn to some subjects of greater importance. Within the course of less than a month I have listened to two speeches from the throne. They ran fairly true to form, in the way in which they were delivered by the gentlemen who represented the crown both here in Ottawa and in Saskatchewan. In Ottawa our new Governor General is the first Canadian-born son to hold this high position. The same is true in Saskatchewan where, for the first time, a speech from the throne was delivered by a native-born son of the province, Mr. W. J. Patterson. Both those appointments were made by this government. I suggest that if everything the government has done was as well accepted as those two appointments, by all political groups, then there would not be any opposition in this house and that would not be a very happy circumstance.
Referring to appointments, I should like to refer to the appointment made by the Department of Labour when it sent Mr. Pat Conroy to Washington to serve as representative of the Canadian government, or of the Department of Labour, in that post. There are trade unions in my constituency. One of those unions happens to consist of coal miners, because at Estevan we have a mine that turns out about one-tenth of all the soft coal produced in Canada. If I might speak for the coal miners in that union I would say vhat the appointment of Mr. Conroy was well Accepted by the boys out there at Estevan. [Mr. Conroy was there at the time of the istrike, and is well known to many of the *miners. On behalf of the miners at the Ester van coal fields I say to the government that the appointment of Mr. Conroy has been well received.
I should like this evening to place some further points before the house for consideration, and in doing so I shall try to be brief. A good deal has been said about the big surplus. I said I would not speak about anything 55704-33}
The Address-Mr. J. J. Smith with which I was not familiar. I am going to make only a few comments about the budget surplus, but I do not make my remarks brief because of a lack of knowledge on the subject.
The figures would seem to indicate that the surplus is somewhere in the neighbourhood of $700 million, and we are told that $400 million of that will be spent before the end of the fiscal year, and the balance paid out on our national debt. I would suppose that members of the official opposition would agree that it is all right to have a surplus; the only difficulty is that they did not put it there.
At this point I should like to quote briefly from a pamphlet in which is set out an article which appeared in the Reader's Digest under the heading "Inflation Concerns Everyone". The article was written by Samuel B. Petten-gill, former democratic congressman from Indiana. I recommend the pamphlet to all hon. members, because I believe it deals with some of the criticisms which have come from some of the opposition benches. What I am about to place on record is the opinion of the congressman, and one with which I certainly agree. He says:
The chief cause of inflation is that the federal government ever since 1930 has spent more than it has taken in.
This is referring to the United States government.
It has gone Into debt during eighteen of the past twenty-one years.
Then further on it says:
One thing the government can and must do is to sop up as much of the increased money supply as possible by taxes. Your part in this is to pay without evasion. Better pay taxes now than have your widow cash in your life insurance some day for just enough to buy a meal-as actually happened in Germany.
That is just about what this government is doing-it is balancing its budget. We hear cries about heavy taxation, but according to that gentleman that is all right. It has been suggested that this heavy taxation is inflationary, but surely no hon. member will suggest that a government or an individual should not pay its debts because it is inflationary. That is all I am going to say about that particular matter.
I should like to say something about foot-and-mouth disease. I spoke about this on another occasion during this session when I suggested that those of us who wanted information should wait until the committee was set up, and the government officials called. Certain gentlemen have indicated a readiness to condemn the officials of the government and the government for what has been done, and I am wondering if they will have the courage to come before that committee and
516	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. J. J. Smith face the officials of the government and the other veterinarians who might be called, and make those same statements. It will be interesting to watch what is done. I am not a member of the agriculture committee but I am certainly going to be there to see what happens.
I have asked myself why it is that we have the foot-and-mouth disease in Saskatchewan. It seems that all disasters fall on that province. If Providence had anything to do with it, why was it permitted to appear in Saskatchewan? The only reason I can think of is that the people of Saskatchewan have great courage. That is the province where men are men and women are sweethearts.
This afternoon the hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Studer) referred to wheat board representation. I understand the board is to be increased from three to five members and we farmers-I am speaking now as a member of the farmers union-feel that the two extra members should be farmers. It is true that farmers do not know everything; it is true that in a farmers organization some radicals will be found; but when you have a practical farmer you have a man of fairly high standing. I am ready to put a practical farmer against a member of any other profession in Canada or any part of the world. It is not necessary to have only professional men. We need some practical farmers on the wheat board. I hope when the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) is making the selections he will see that the added representation is made up of practical farmers.
I want to say a word about the automobile industry. We have heard a lot about this industry in the last few years, more particularly this last winter. I have an opinion about the automobile industry and I say at once that it is a personal opinion. However, when I have an opinion I do not hesitate to express it before this house. I came across a rather interesting book not long ago giving facts and figures of the automobile industry, the 1951 edition. This was issued by the Canadian Automobile Chamber of Commerce.
We have heard a lot about this infant automobile industry. It has been coddled and nursed and protected for years and I suggest that it has now grown up. It is a big boy now and it is time it stood on its own feet. It does not need any more protection. My Conservative friends-I do not include the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) at this time- will say: "What about the automobile industry? It needs protection." That may be their reason, but I do not agree with them. As I say, this industry has had time to grow up.


My mind goes back to the time when the customs duties were taken off farm machinery, I believe in 1927 and 1936. When that was done we heard great cries about the implement companies being ruined, but that has not turned out to be the case. The financial reports indicate that these companies are doing fairly well. There is no difference in the automobile industry. That industry should be able to stand on its own feet and compete with automobiles from other countries.
The importation of cars not manufactured in the year of import is prohibited. I do not think that should be. Let us consider some figures given in the book to which I just referred. I do not like messing up my speech with a lot of figures, but I have some here which I think will be rather interesting. The automotive production in 1950 was 284,000 passenger cars, 106,000 trucks and buses, or a total of 390,000 units. That was nearly 100,000 more than had been produced in 1949, or an increase of 50 per cent. In 1950 the financed sales were 31-5 per cent of the total, the balance being cash sales. In other words, about one-third of the sales were financed and two-thirds were for cash. There were more cars sold for cash in 1950 than were produced in 1949. I suggest to the government to give serious consideration to taking off all duties on automobiles entering Canada. I think it will be found that, as I have said, this industry has grown up and is able to look after itself.
It is true that some retailers or car agents are in difficulty, but why is this? They acted on bad advice from the automobile industry which forced them to build large garages, show rooms and so on. Many dealers went into the thing too heavily and are now in trouble. It might be noted that the tax on automobiles imposed in Canada is far out of line with what is paid in the United States. It is not necessary for me to give my arguments to the minister as he has heard them in another place. I trust that in his new budget the minister will give some consideration to getting that tax in line with the one in the United States. If he is unable to do so, I hope he will tell us why.	J
In conclusion, I have one other point I wish to bring to the attention of the house. It concerns the war bonds that were sold during the last war. Some of the people in this dominion are today forced to sell those bonds to enable them to buy food. The bond salesmen told these purchasers that these bonds were the best investment they could make. The people were told to be patriotic and buy a bond. I have some of these bonds, not too many. I am not speaking for myself

The Address-Mr. Cloutier
because I hope I shall be able to hold these bonds until maturity, at which time I shall get one hundred cents on the dollar plus interest. They have not been a bad investment, but there are many people in Canada who bought those bonds and who knew quite well that they could not hold them until maturity. Many of the old people expected that they would be dead before that time. Some of the people who are forced to sell their bonds today are taking around 95 cents on the dollar, and I do not think that is good enough. I would ask the minister to give the house some explanation why the government cannot make these bonds sell at par, the same as the Canadian savings bonds.
The minister is in the fortunate position of having a surplus this year. We are having good times, taxes are easily collected and money is fairly free. We are now in a cold war. If we have to continue this cold war too long and economic conditions become difficult, then taxes will not come in so freely. If we get into a shooting war, we may have to go into the market and sell government bonds again. I am afraid that it is going to be rather difficult to sell government bonds when people know quite well that many of those who bought them during the last war are not getting 100 cents on the dollar.
There is a little more in this article which I should like to quote.
If I save money by useful work, producing goods which others have bought, and lend $1,000-my savings-to Uncle Sam, there has been no increase in the nation's money supply. Uncle Sam has $1,000 more; I have $1,000 less. But if the government borrows $1,000 from a commercial bank, the money supply of the nation has increased by that amount. The bank takes Uncle Sam's promissory note, a government bond, and credits him with a $1,000 deposit against which he draws checks to pay his bills.
In my opinion as long as the government borrows money from its own people-we are referring to Canada now-then that government is no poorer. If it has to borrow money even from the banks, that creates more money and makes inflation. I would suggest that the government might try to make it possible to give these people 100 cents on the dollar who have to cash their bonds now in order to live. As I have said, I hope that the Minister of Finance will be able to tell us why he cannot do anything about cutting some of this taxation on automobiles, if that is not possible. I hope he will be able to tell us why something cannot be done about these war bonds to see that these people get back 100 cents on the dollar. So far as removing the duty on automobiles coming into this country is concerned, I would advise him not to tell us why
it should not be done because there is no explanation. The government should just remove the duty.

Mr. Speaker, I am unable to restrain strong emotions as I rise in this house, to speak on behalf of the constituents of Drum-mond-Arthabaska whom I have the honour to represent in the Canadian House of Commons.
The emotion I feel springs from various motives; to start with, I would say that it is inspired by the fact that the constituency of Drummond-Arthabaska has known many very great politicians; I wish I were as eloquent today as were Laurier, LaVergne, Dorion and other great orators; thus, the voice of my constituency could be heard in this chamber with the brilliancy and the eloquence of former days!
I would have to be a poet to do justice to the constituency I represent. For I feel that Drummond-Arthabaska is no ordinary riding and it is the very breath of its soul which vibrates today in the recesses of my own heart.
There are several reasons why we should pay special attention to Drummond-Arthabaska. May I first of all mention the part the constituency played during the last war when it placed first in the victory loan campaigns held throughout Canada. The understanding prevailing in our plants between employers and employees should also be held as a model. We have very large industries as well as several private concerns that are quite prosperous. Everywhere there is harmony between English and Frenchspeaking citizens as well as between the various classes of society. Have we not there a reflection of our national life?
I would be remiss in my duty if I failed to mention the farmers of my county with whom I remain in close relationship. Those who remain faithful to the land deserve that we take an interest in their fate. There are several problems that I should like to mention here. Let us not forget that the farmer remains the cornerstone of society, the hope of tomorrow and of the future.
Since my election as member for Drummond-Arthabaska, I had made it a point to make one or two speeches during each session. Some will no doubt wonder why I have not yet spoken since my re-election in 1949. If I have not spoken sooner it is because the esteem and respect I have for my new colleagues prompted me to await my turn so that they would expound their views and policies.

The Address-Mr. Cloutier I avail myself of this opportunity to pay tribute to present members of parliament, who are undoubtedly the most active ever seen in this house.
I also wish to congratulate my distinguished colleagues, the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Gentlemen, you have fulfilled your duty in a very remarkable manner.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, so many of my colleagues speak English that I shall continue in their language, with which I am not so familiar as it is not my mother tongue. I therefore beg your indulgence, Mr. Speaker, and that of the house.
I avail myself of this opportunity to pay a public and respectful tribute to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and to present to him the usual compliments, as well as to assure him of my most sincere admiration and attachment. His predecessor, Right Hon. Mackenzie King, left him a happy if difficult legacy in view of these troublesome times. He knows, however, how to fulfil this task. Thanks to his talents as a great lawyer, as a fair and just man and as an administrator, he has surrounded himself with eminent colleagues such as the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) whom I should call this country's great builder since, under his skilful direction, Canada has become the fourth world power. I should also mention the right hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) who has so long devoted his talents, his experience, his oratorical skill and his persuasiveness to furthering the interests of the agricultural community.
It would take too long to mention each and every department, but I would like to underscore the personal integrity, the diligence and the very high qualifications of the members of the cabinet as well as their parliamentary assistants. All contribute in splendid fashion to make Canada one of the best organized powers in the world. On behalf of my constituents I therefore wish to pay tribute to these hon. gentlemen, and to thank them for the excellent co-operation they have never failed to extend in furthering the interests and the general welfare of the constituency of Drummond-Arthabaska.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, you will permit me to sound a note of sadness. In all the countries of the commonwealth 1952 is a year of mourning for our glorious monarch. He will be remembered as a very worthy king, both as a man of duty and a man possessed of great family virtues. In this connection I

wish to quote an editorial signed by Mr. Louis-Philippe Roy, editor of L'Action Catholique of Quebec city, who wrote:
AH his life George VI was a man of duty. There is no greater virtue than to perform one's task everywhere and all the time, whether it be obscure or exalted. It would moreover be ridiculous to believe that the kingly office has ini it nothing but glory, adulation and receptions. During the last war, as on numerous other occasions, the deceased monarch showed how human he had remained, how close to his subjects whose worries, hardships and sufferings he shared. These tragic tidings deeply affect all those countries over which George VI reigned, because it is the holder of authority who disappears; but if this sorrow is genuinely heartfelt it is because, under the kingly trappings, beat the heart of a father. The king was in truth the beloved father of a fine family. And therein most certainly lies the second lesson to be drawn from his life. Never did the splendours of the palace eclipse for him the more domestic happiness of a united Christian family.
Honesty of mind, gentleness of character, simplicity of demeanour, personal integrity; all these the Canadian people had occasion to observe in the person of this monarch who visited Canada in 1939. We therefore take our share of the understandable affliction of the royal family. We will make it our duty to pray for the deceased sovereign, for the noble queen who survives him and more especially for Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II who acceded to the throne. It is all the easier to wish Her Majesty a peaceful and glorious reign since she has just concluded in this country a tour which accorded us the occasion of admiring in her person the qualities of her noble father, and above all, perhaps, the character of Victoria, her illustrious forebear. May God bless the royal family in its present bereavement as well as in the glamour of this glorious accession to the throne.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, may God bless the royal family. Such is the hope I am expressing on behalf of the constituency I represent and especially of the city of Drummondville, which in November of 1951 was honoured by the official visit of Their Royal Highnesses The Princess Elizabeth and the Duke of Edinburgh.
Another event which took place almost at the beginning of 1952 was the departure of His Excellency the Viscount Alexander of Tunis and his family. It must be emphasized that Viscount Alexander was, par excellence, the transition governor. Indeed., no royal representative was more Canadian than he; none of his predecessors had better understood the bi-racial and cultural character of this country. Viscount Alexander of Tunis will be remembered by all Canadians, both French and English-speaking, as a man who understood our country, who loved its people and who contributed largely to preparing that happy transition brought about by his departure for his mother country, where he has gone to assume important duties.
His Excellency the Right Hon. Vincent Massey, who succeeds Viscount Alexander of Tunis, will be the fifty-sixth governor general of Canada, in a succession of governors that

goes back to Samuel de Champlain, who was appointed as governor of New France in 1633. His Excellency will be the eighteenth governor general since confederation and the first Canadian to be appointed to this high office since the signing of this historic agreement. The investigation he led into the development of the arts, letters and sciences in Canada was to prepare him further for the high honour and heavy responsibility placed upon him. His Excellency the Right Hon. Vincent Massey has shown unequivocally and bravely that he too has understood the bi-racial and cultural character of Canada and its spiritual mission throughout the world. [DOT]
On behalf of all the electors I represent, I wish His Excellency the Right Hon. Vincent Massey success in his new responsibilities.
I was saying, gentlemen, that Canada, under the leadership of the present government, has become one of the best organized powers, as much by its freedoms, the privileges enjoyed by its citizens, its labour organizations, and its social security measures as by its resources, its economic development and, above all, by the part it has come to play in the international sphere, by its diplomacy, and its contribution to the various bodies entrusted with safeguarding "peace". Indeed, our country-as has often been pointed out by the Prime Minister-wants peace and not war! But it must be in a position to offer some resistance to the enemy; to that end, I am convinced that, according to the old saying, if we want peace, we must prepare for war: si vis pacem, para bellum.
It also appears to me that any unfair aggression should be checked and that is the reason why we have sent a brigade to Korea. With all my colleagues, I deeply deplore the death of those who have fallen on the battlefields, although casualties have been relatively low since there are only, thus far, 127 dead, 514 wounded and 5 missing. Despite the fact that the war goes on-which is very deeply regretted by all-those figures are not at all excessive.
In fact, I believe that the city of Drummond ville has lost only two or three of its sons in Korea, among whom there is unfortunately a man whom I considered as one of my warm personal friends, a very devoted and likeable figure, who knew how to sustain our boys' courage. I refer to Major Rosaire Lupien, one of my fellow citizens, who had the honour of being appointed principal chaplain of all the forces of the commonwealth in Korea. And this, after he had played an active and courageous part during the last war on the main battlefields of Europe!
The Address-Mr. Cloutier
Here are the words of the New Year's message which was sent to me by my excellent friend, Major Lupien, and it is with the deepest emotion that I quote:
I have deeply appreciated in this far away place the good wishes you have sent me. The letter you wrote to my father in connection with my recent promotion has caused him much pleasure. Please accept in return my religious wishes for the New Year.
A few days ago the Hon. Messrs. Claxton and Lapointe were in Korea; I had the honour of conversing with both of them.
My health is excellent and all is well.
Religiously yours,
Korea, January 4, 1952.
Rosaire Lupien, priest.
Army Chaplain.
Is that not, Mr. Speaker, a very moving echo of the great morale of that brave apostle, of that priest and soldier who spared neither his zeal nor his devotion to hold up the courage of those who were committed to his care. That is why I wished to pay officially to Major Lupien my most respectful and loyal tribute and may I be permitted to extend this tribute to the good family of my late distinguished fellow citizen.
But since I am now talking about our men in foreign lands, I wish to repeat a request which I have already had the honour of making in this house. In fact with what fervour and impulse wouldn't the hearts of our boys thrill if they had been given a symbol of their country, the flag. "The flag" calls forth courage and discipline; it bears in its folds the salvation and glory of a people.
Why, gentlemen, I ask you, should Canadians be left any longer without a standard? Canada has truly become a nation which should have "its flag", an emblem to represent her not only as a free people but also as a power to be reckoned with.
Nothing great will be accomplished if the whole soul of a nation does not breathe in the folds of a common flag. The spirit is everything and the sense of the ideal and the divine in man, and in society, of that which transcends the life of the individual, and gives it its value, vibrates in a flag, is carried in its folds over the wide spaces and beyond the seas, a symbol of self-respect and justifiable national pride.
Let us hope that in the very near future Canada will have a truly national and distinctive flag, a standard, an oriflamme which will find its place among the most beautiful, the most respected and the most beloved national emblems, the world over!
It is only logical that the idea of a national anthem should be linked with that of a flag, and, here again, I must voice for the second
520	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Cloutier time in this house the regret that a national anthem has not yet been adopted. I do not see why we should not simply decide in favour of "O Canada", since all the virtues it extols belong equally to each of the two groups which make up our country!
The soul of a nation expresses itself through its national anthem, the beauty of which is in direct relation to the nobleness of the feelings it conveys. Could there be a better choice than that of "O Canada", this inspiring hymn, flowing from the source, the very heart of a religious and heroic race, an anthem of pride and hope, a song extolling our tenacity, our bravery, qualities which are still admired overseas on the battle front, the war song par excellence:
Canada was born of a proud nation Thy history is an epic poem Relating the most brilliant deeds!
Our national anthem "O Canada" is not only a recalling of the past, it is an inspiration for the future, and it is easy to interpret it as the inspiring symbol of Canadian unity: Let us be a nation of brothers Under the bond of Faith!
Let us sing out as our fathers did
The victorious cry: "For God and the King!"
"O Canada" is the hymn, the very anthem of our country, rising from the soil and which is echoed back as the thrilling voice of the past and the dynamic voice of the future by our great rivers and our immense forests from the east to the west. As I have said, "O Canada" should remain our national anthem, for no other hymn can better express "the soul of our country." It reflects the past, the present and the future, the very aspirations of a vast, of an immense country. As someone so rightly said the day "O Canada" is sung from Newfoundland and: Cape Breton to Vancouver and Victoria our Canadian nation will have made much progress towards the union of hearts and minds.
These young Canadians from both racial groups who some years ago took part in a forum on Canadian unity came to the following conclusion: "Canada can become a nation only if she achieves a common purpose. The other provinces must understand Quebec at least as well as Quebec understands them. And Quebec, for her part, must realize that she is the most difficult part of Canada to understand."
In the past twenty-five years we have no doubt made constant progress along the path to Canadian unity, And as was stated by the hon. Senator Adelard Godbout, it was during those years when national unity was at its peak that Canada achieved the greatest strides in the economic as well as the military and international fields.


We therefore have everything to gain by fostering closer relations between our two races. Who are the French Canadians? Colonel Goforth, director general of the Canadian army general staff in Ottawa, during the last war, asked that question and answered it in a very eloquent manner. Here is what he said of the French Canadians:
They came from small villages in Normandy, Brittany, on the other side of the narrow sea that separated them from the native country of our ancestors. The French expression "La Manche" brings something very suggestive to our minds, because it compares that sea to Neptune's sleeve. In that imaginative sense, those of us who are of English descent and have received an important adjunction of Norman and Celtic blood, are made of the same stuff from that same sleeve as those with whom we share this Canada of ours.
And Colonel Goforth points out that history books give no information about everyday life and the thoughts of the people which really constitute the history of a nation. The glorious tradition, Mr. Speaker, of Canadian arms did not begin with Wolfe's victory on the plains of Abraham, but with the heroic struggle of a tiny band of French colonists against an enemy. The desperate and never to be forgotten resistance of Dollard, Sieur des Ormeaux, and of his comrades on t'he shares of the Ottawa river, is as much an epic in our history as the heroic deeds of Cecil Merritt at Dieppe or Paul Triquet at Casa Berardi.
When our Canadian soil was invaded during the revolutionary war and again in 1812, it was the unswerving loyalty of New France towards the British crown and the heroic deeds of her sons, de Salaberry for instance, which laid the foundations for the future glory of Canada. For more than a century our French-speaking fellow countrymen have always found a noble and inspired leader who understood the value and necessity of Canadian unity, who rallied his own people and ours to his own vision of our common destiny, who successfully toiled to communicate this ideal to those of his generation. These leaders were not men of the same political party. The first was Sir Louis Hippolyte Lafontaine, whose association with Baldwin created the happy union of Upper and Lower Canada. Then at the time of confederation under Sir John A. Macdonald's quite long administration, it was the well-balanced leadership of Sir Georges-Etienne Cartier and Hector Langevin which preserved the harmonious agreement between Quebec and the other components of the new dominion. The era of Sir Wilfrid Laurier might be called the golden era of Canada's growth and prosperity. The fires of racial language and religious prejudices never

The Address-Mr. Cloutier
burned less fiercely in all our history, while the light of our patriotism shines with renewed glory.
To these names which recall the political milestones of Canadian history, Baldwin, Macdonald, Lafontaine, Cartier, Laurier, must immediately be added another sympathetic and recent figure, whose prestige at once appeals to the imagination; I mean the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King. His memory remains dear and ever alive, not only to his followers and to those who knew and loved him, but also to all Canadians, whatever their social class or their religious and political convictions.
"William Lyon Mackenzie King," it has been said, "what a marvellous name to add to the greatest and most brilliant names forever inscribed in the annals of Canadian history!" His predecessors Macdonald and Laurier in particular had played an important part in the triumph of responsible government, national unity and the development of Canadian autonomy. Well, the Right Hon. Mr. King, by a slow and difficult, but sure and successful process, has obtained for us the statute, universally recognized today, of a free and powerful nation and, may I add, has led us to a point very near to full autonomy.
Indeed, the Right Hon. Mackenzie King, in most difficult times and in circumstances which might have riven the country in two irreconcilable blocs, contributed more than anyone else to the unity of Canada. He found a nation sorely divided, riven by the controversies of the first war, torn by political disputes, which set east against west and race against race. Nevertheless he was called after his death, and rightly so, "the man of peace, the greatest single force for a united Canada."
The Right Hon. Mackenzie King, in an extremely serious and critical period, achieved the miracle of national unity. Under the able guidance of this great leader, Canada has become in the climax of his leadership not only a power but a great power, with a wealth of destiny still before it in the world.
William Lyon Mackenzie King immediately takes his place among the great leaders who helped to fashion the destinies of Canada, our young and beautiful country. And I suggest it is fitting that we honour his memory as soon as possible.
A group of distinguished Canadian citizens are at present seeing to it that a monument is erected in Montreal to the memory of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the great French-Canadian statesman whose constituency I have the honour to represent in this house.
May I be permitted to express the wish that on a prominent spot on parliament hill there may soon be erected, to the memory of the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, a monument of bronze, of brass or perhaps of marble, which will recall the sympathetic and familiar features of the great lamented man whose moving as well as indestructible memory lies in the hearts of all our people.
If I take the liberty of bringing forth today such a request, possibly it is because I was favoured with a particularly gracious gesture on the part of the Right Hon. Mackenzie King, who was most sympathetic and friendly towards me. And I remember that other speech on national unity I delivered a few years ago, on the occasion of which I received words of congratulation from Mr. King, to the effect that I was imbued with true Canadian spirit, the very spirit that inspired such great men as Laurier and other outstanding statesmen. I did not think the incident would have any repercussions, but a few days later I had the privilege of being called to a private meeting where I was warmly received and of which I retain-need I add-an unforgettable and very touching memory.
Therefore, in view of the interest which the Right Hon. Mackenzie King seemed to have taken in that speech, may I conclude by referring to the broad picture which Canadian unity had evoked in my mind, and which the mention of those great statesmen from Lafontaine and Baldwin to Laurier and Mackenzie King recalled to my memory; that gigantic country of ours, Canada, which covers the whole St. Lawrence valley, Newfoundland, this new Canadian province which has sent us such worthy representatives, the fertile lands from the bay of Fundy to the great lakes region, the western prairies, the Rockies, and the lands bordering the great Pacific ocean.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, may I quote again from the works of one of our Canadian poets these few lines from "The Mixer", whose meaning reaches the very depths of my soul, and which I should like to share with you:
In the city, on the prairies, in the forest, in the camp,
In the mountain-clouds of colour, in the fog-white river-damp,
From Atlantic to Pacific, from the great lakes to the pole,
I am mixing strange ingredients into a common whole,
Every hope shall build upon me, every heart shall be my own,
The ambition of my people shall be mine and mine alone,

The Address-Mr. Dinsdale Through the pangs of transformation in my fiery furnace blast,
Do I shape and mould and make them "Canadian at last."
