speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a speech which I never expected to have to deliver in this chamber. It deals with a subject that, from the standpoint of logic and good common sense, I feel should have the support of all hon. members of the house. Unfortunately, notwithstanding that fact it seems that the government has decided to discontinue the annual grant of $15,000 to the international peace garden, and I wish to take this opportunity of bringing a few thoughts before hon. members of the house on that subject.
From another standpoint I think it is fortunate that this opportunity is afforded because, as I have discussed this topic with some members of the house, it would appear that the purpose and history of the international peace garden is little known. I should hope that the discussion which will take place around this subject may provide the necessary publicity, not only in this chamber but right across this great dominion of ours.
The debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne has revolved mostly around domestic problems. It is only indirectly that we have become involved in discussions outside the immediate matters facing government in connection with the governing of the country. We have launched into the field of external affairs briefly, and it becomes increasingly obvious that there is the area wherein lies the real difficulty. I am sure we all feel that unless we solve the problem of external relations, unless we deal with the matter of living peaceably together in the great society into which we have been precipitated by modern means of communication and transportation, all the solutions proposed in this chamber towards the settling of domestic problems such as inflation, high taxes, unemployment-or what have you- will be of little import.
The preamble to the United Nations charter says something to this effect, that wars are made in the minds of men, and it is in the minds of men that the defences of peace must be built. That is a very idealistic and high-sounding phrase; yet, nevertheless, it is true. The difficulty is that of building these positive defences of peace in the minds of men and women not only in this country but in all other nations of the world at the present time.
We know there are movements afoot supposedly promoting the idea of peace and

international understanding. Certain representations were made to hon. members at the time of the session last fall by a movement which professes to promote peace but which, to my way of thinking and, I believe, to the way of thinking of all hon. members in this chamber, can be described only as the peace which passeth all understanding. Peace is a very difficult ideal to promote, and I feel that one of the major functions, if not indeed the major function of the whole international peace garden idea, is to provide a symbol of peace around which the thinking of the people of Canada, the people of the United States and the peoples of other countries in the world can revolve.
It provides that symbol. We are all aware of the powerful influences symbols have; we are well aware of their powerful emotional effect upon the thinking of mankind. We need refer only to symbols such as the national flag, and the devotion and patriotism that is aroused whenever it appears. Then, so far as the Christian religion is concerned, we need refer only to the symbol of the cross. On a much less exalted level, we remember the powerful influence wielded by the symbol of the swastika-the double cross -in moulding the thinking of the people in Hitler's Germany.
I should like to give hon. members some information concerning this peace garden project. It began in the mind of one man. The whole idea was conceived in 1928 by the late Dr. Henry J. Moore of Islington, Ontario, an internationally known horticulturist. He presented his idea to a meeting of the international garden association being held in Toronto and it was enthusiastically picked up by that group. In 1931 the International Peace Garden Association was formed consisting of citizens from Canada and the United States, mainly representatives from the eastern parts of these two countries.
That association began to look for a suitable site for the peace garden. At first interest was focused on certain park areas in the east and then attention was focused on the far west. The central region was ignored because, as was said by one member of the association from the state of New York, it was thought there was nothing that would possibly be suitable in that God-forsaken frozen north country. But strangely enough after the committee visited the Turtle mountain region on the border between Manitoba and North Dakota it immediately saw the natural possibilities of that area and in 1931

that site was selected and arrangements went forward immediately for the implementation of the peace garden idea.
On July 14, 1932, I believe it was, the opening ceremonies in connection with the international peace garden occurred. I was present myself. The road leading into the garden from both sides of the border was merely a country trail at that time. In spite of the transportation difficulties and the fact that the idea was relatively new, some 50,000 people gathered to take part in the dedication ceremonies. It was typical of the peace garden movement right from the beginning that such vast numbers of people should be interested for it will be readily understood that the desire for peace is deep-rooted and sincere in the hearts of all people.
As I see it, there are three main functions of this peace garden. First, it recognizes the fact that a unique situation exists in an unguarded frontier of three thousand miles between the United States and Canada. Second, it promotes the general idea of peace. To symbolize this in a beautiful garden is I think an excellent idea. Going back to the beginning of man's pilgrimage on this earth we automatically think of the idyllic state established in the garden of Eden. No better symbolism than that of a garden could have been selected to promote the intangible idea of peace. Then it provides something concrete, something tangible around which the hopes of mankind can be oriented.
In addition to the idealistic aspect of the garden, there are certain practical and utilitarian considerations. I have no doubt that in arriving at the decision to withdraw support, financial, materialistic, and practical considerations were uppermost. I mentioned that when the garden was first established in 1932 there was just a country trail into the area; but today the garden is transversed by a modern paved highway approaching from both the north and the south. In the relatively short period of its development the international peace garden has become a significant tourist attraction. This garden is on the famous Cape to Churchill highway. Mr. M. J. Tinline, who following his retirement from his position as superintendent of the experimental farm at Brandon has enthusiastically given of his services in promoting the peace garden, in a recent speech had this to say about the garden as a tourist attraction:
The great garden will be on the Canada to canal highway at a point on the international boundary between Dunseith, N.D., and Boissevain, Manitoba, and sixty miles south of Brandon. The location is almost the exact centre between the Atlantic and Pacific and but thirty miles north of the exact centre of the North American continent which is at Rugby, N.D. The highway extends from a point
55704-34J
The Address-Mr. Dinsdale two hundred miles north of the boundary to the Panama canal, and it is to extend north to Churchill and south to Cape Horn. Upon this main street of the Americas, which will be the longest north and south highway in the world, will travel millions of people in the days to come.
The highway, it is hoped, will link the garden of peace with the monument, Christ of the Andes, erected by the Argentine and Chilian governments on their boundary in 1904.
Because of the increasing significance of the garden as a tourist attraction there is a movement afoot on both sides of the boundary to establish more adequate customs facilities. The United States congress has appropriated $90,000 to bring the American facilities into line with the present tourist needs and I understand the Canadian government is contemplating similar action. While we are dealing with the practical aspect of the garden I think it would be well to note a statement by the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) appearing in the Ottawa Journal this evening to the effect that last year Canada had an estimated deficit of $9 million in her tourist trade. I venture to predict that, as the symbolism and significance of the peace garden idea establishes itself in the thinking of the people, the relatively insignificant $15,000 which has been provided each year since 1949 will be repaid many times. Tourists are visiting this garden in increasing numbers because they realize that it is a unique manifestation of a wonderful idea. It is beginning to attract pilgrims from all over the world.
Last June and July in a place which twenty years ago was a mere wilderness there were 30,000 visitors reported in at the customs station. This is simply an indication of the attraction that this garden will be to tourists if the development which has been going on so satisfactorily is allowed to continue.
It must be admitted that even though the garden idea was first launched twenty years ago the development has been relatively slow. It was conceived during the depression. During all the years of the depression, the only assistance provided was through the United States civilian conservation corps and men from our Canadian relief camps. They did some of the basic work of construction, road building, tree removal and planting and so forth. It was not until the late member for Brandon, Mr. J. E. Matthews, began to take a personal interest in the garden following the years of world war II-when of course most developments of this kind were at a standstill-that the development really began to make progress. I am told that he was instrumental in bringing the matter so forcibly to the attention of the government that the $15,000 grant was first provided in 1949. In turn, he appeared before the United States

The Address-Mr. Dinsdale congress and succeeded, along with others, in having a grant of $100,000 provided from the United States counterpart of this house.
I feel that, in a sense, the peace garden development is a personal memorial to my predecessor in this house. I would add that that is one of the main reasons why I am picking up the torch on behalf of this project.
What will be the result of the withdrawal of support at this time? Work recently accomplished, particularly within the last two years, is going to be undone because the retaining walls have still not been built. This construction work was on the agenda for the current year. Soil erosion is going to remove most of the beneficial effects of some of these developments. There is the possibility also that the withdrawal of Canadian support will see a declining interest so far as the United States congress is concerned.
Supposedly, the whole move is in the interest of economy. I should like to suggest, Mr. Speaker, that there are much easier ways of effecting economies, if that is the desire of the government, without detracting from this important project in the interests of international understanding and peace. For example, we have had instances brought before the house of government expenditures for rentals in the city of Ottawa for space that was never used amounting to some $70,000. This is far beyond the $15,000 involved in the annual grant. Then, we move into the area of defence expenditures. I would venture to prophesy that when the committee on defence expenditures begins its deliberations, many instances will be revealed of unnecessary expenditures far greater than this relatively small amount. It is ridiculously small when placed alongside the astronomical figures in which governments indulge today.
A final argument on behalf of the peace garden, and maybe the most effective argument, is the fact that women's groups right across this country have had their imaginations captivated by the idealism and symbolism involved. Such groups as the women's institutes, the Red Cross association, the I.O.D.E., the Professional and Business Women and similar groups on the other side of the border have been promoting plots in the garden area. They are going to be very disappointed when they discover that the relatively small support that has been coming from the dominion government is going to be withdrawn during this critical period of development. I think there is an old quotation to the effect that hell hath no fury like a woman scorned. I only hope that the ladies demonstrate such fury as they have never done before when they raise a protest over the withdrawal of support for this project.

To bring my remarks to a conclusion, I think that here is a real test of the true spirit of democracy. If the government of Canada cannot find the wherewithal for this infinitesimal sum of $15,000 for the promotion of the ideal of peace, we will be very remiss in our duty as responsible representatives of the people. Rather than withdraw support, I feel we should be speaking in terms of increasing the support so that we might give all the encouragement possible to the few who have worked so valiantly towards the realization of the dream of the late Dr. Henry Moore. If necessary, these appropriations might come out of the Department of National Defence, which is dealing today in billions and not thousands of dollars. If we can afford millions of dollars for armaments for the negative aspect of of defence, surely we can afford $15,000 for the promotion of the one idea in this country that is so successfully building the spiritual bulwarks of peace in the minds of men everywhere.

I did not intend to speak again in this debate, but there were certain remarks made by the member for Maple Creek (Mr. Studer) this afternoon that we in this group cannot allow to go unanswered.

speechtext:
We can take it all right, but we like facts. If I remember correctly, when speaking on a previous occasion the member for Maple Creek said that he had several brothers in the United States who could speak longer and faster than he could. Well, he made a pretty good job himself. We do not mind his speaking at length and speaking quickly, but in this group we do like to listen to facts. Owing to foot-and-mouth disease

in Saskatchewan, the concern over redistribution and the tension that is being developed with the coming provincial election, possibly the hon. member was not in his usual normal condition. In the words of a well-known Victorian statesman, it is quite safe to say that this afternoon he was completely intoxicated with the exuberance of his own verbosity.
I should like to refer to a few statements the hon. member made as we noted them at this end of the house. The member made general remarks. His speech was largely generalities, except that part in which he was trying to score on the C.C.F. members in this house.
At one point in referring to the C.C.F. members the hon. member said, "I would say they are conditional Canadians." We in this group cannot permit that slander to go unanswered, a slander not only on the members of this group but on hundreds of thousands of good Canadians in this country. When a person says we are conditional Canadians, according to the dictionary meaning of the word he says our loyalty is limited by certain factors, that it is conditioned by certain circumstances. Well, Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is much necessity for me to tell this house that the loyalty of this group goes unchallenged in Canada.
I do not bring these facts to the attention of the house by way of boasting. We recognize that some members of the house served in one sphere while some served in others. I am not making these remarks as any reflection upon those who did not have the opportunity to serve in His Majesty's armed forces; but I would bring to the attention of the house the fact that this valiant little group-and I think it has to be valiant to submit to the torrent of words of criticism we listen to at times-has the second highest percentage of members who served in the front line of any of the groups in this house. Of this group 38-64 per cent served in the front line in the first or second world wars. The ancestors of the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright), our national chairman, came to this country in 1790. The family of the hon. member for Maple Creek arrived quite recently in comparison with them. I understand that in Quebec there is a small town or village named Wrightville, after the ancestors of the hon. member for Melfort. He also served overseas with distinction in the first world war, and his son served in the second world war. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) served overseas with the Canadian expeditionary force in the first world war, and was severely wounded. The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) served with the famous
The Address-Mr. Herridge 51st highland division in the first world war. The hon. member for Yale (Mr. Jones) served in the first world war and was wounded. All these hon. members joined up in the early days of that war. Then coming to the member for Kootenay West, he had some little part in the first world hostilities. His wife served as a nursing sister overseas for three years. His father served in two wars, and three of his daughters served in the second world war.
So I do not think anyone can refer to the members of this group as conditional Canadians. We have done our best to demonstrate our loyalty to this country and our willingness to defend it when its interests are at stake. I want to remind the house also that in the federal election of 1945 the C.C.F. received the largest percentage of the soldiers' vote from overseas. It is obvious that the troops overseas did not consider those running on the C.C.F. ticket as conditional Canadians. I would like also to remind hon. members opposite that the late prime minister was defeated by a C.C.F. candidate in the constituency of Prince Albert by the overseas military vote.
Then at one point in his speech the hon. member for Maple Creek said, "The C.C.F. supported the war when Russia came in." That is completely untrue, as the record will prove. I want to quote very briefly from Hansard of September 9, 1939, at page 55. This is just one paragraph from the speech of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell):
The Co-operative Commonwealth Federation recognizes that Canada is now implicated in a struggle which may involve the survival of democratic institutions. We consider that in the cause of the allied powers lies a hope of building European peace on a more secure foundation because, in part at least, the people of Britain and France are waging a war against aggression.
Surely that proves the position of this movement at the commencement of the war. On that occasion the late J. S. Woodsworth, whose memory is very much respected by representatives of all parties in this country, voted against the war appropriations because he was a confirmed pacifist on principle. At the same time there were Liberal members who voted against the war appropriations. I presume they expressed their convictions and took that action because of their principles. We do not suggest for a moment that they were conditional Canadians.
At another point in his remarks the hon. member for Maple Creek said, "The socialist policy is not a Canadian policy." Well, our foundation policy is the Regina manifesto, which expresses the philosophy of the C.C.F. It was drafted by Canadians to suit Canadian conditions and Canadian circumstances. It is
526	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Herridge a completely Canadian product, drafted as the result of the meeting together of representatives of labour and farmers across the country, of people in the universities, professional and business groups and others. In that connection the hon. member also said that was why we did not owe allegiance to any country, that we were committed to world revolution. Anyone who has studied Canadian political history knows that is completely nonsensical. I presume the hon. member spoke without knowledge and in some confusion, but I want to deal with that point. I happen to have in my hand the transcript of an address given by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar on Friday, March 14, to the American study group of Amherst college. The title is "The case for an evolutionary socialism". This is what the hon. member had to say quite recently, and it has been said over and over again; the point of view of this party has been expressed both in this house and across the country, but I want to quote this because I think it is a good antidote to the misstatement of fact by the hon. member for Maple Creek. Intelligent people would not accept his statement as a fact, but there may be some people without knowledge who would think there was something in what he had to say. Mr. Coldwell's address contained these words:
Evolutionary, democratic or, as it is sometimes called. Fabian socialism, particularly as it is understood and advocated in the United Kingdom, throughout the commonwealth of nations and northwest Europe, and by others in the United States, is the product of a distinctly evolutionary process. It rejects the methods of communism which rely on revolutionary and catastrophic upheavals to attain its ends. Democratic socialism, therefore, emphatically repudiates the use of force as a desirable instrument of social and economic change. Thus it is not only distinguishable from modern communism but from some other movements which, in the past and I fear to some extent in the present, prostitute the word "socialist." Such parties, of course, were Mussolini's fascist party in Italy and Hitler's national socialist party in Germany.
Because democratic socialism has reached its greatest strength and influence in the United Kingdom and other countries with parliamentary institutions of the British type, I shall describe briefly the background of our movement. Historically, and most readily from British sources, this development can be traced from the medieval socialism of the guilds and monastic orders through the Tudor and Stuart periods of the mercantile era to the eighteenth century and the beginning of the industrial revolution.

If I could have permission,
I can finish in a couple of minutes.
From this revolution in industry, capitalism developed great productive forces . . .


This ultimate goal, to be attained by evolutionary means-
Then I want to deal briefly with another quotation from this speech by Mr. Coldwell:
Totalitarianism, whether of the communist or fascist variety, outrages human dignity because it denies these basic moral values of individual personality and freedom; on the other hand our indictment against capitalism is that it has denied to great masses of people-particularly when there is a period of overproduction-the right to consume and enjoy the products of their toil. We believe that our objectives can only be secured by well-defined and progressive steps taken with and by the consent of the people exercising their franchise democratically. Wherever there is a denial of these rights, there can be no real freedom and democracy.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, once again we have indicated the philosophy of this movement; these basic socialist principles are unchangeable and have been unchanged since the movement was established in this country.
Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I want to deal with one other statement. The hon. member said that the premier of one province stated that they were not prepared to send their sons to be slaughtered to bolster discredited regimes. What is wrong with that statement? Is the hon. member willing to send the sons of Canada to bolster discredited regimes? We send our sons to fight aggression and to make certain that democratic regimes are established when peace is secured.
I had a few more remarks that I intended to make at this time, but I think I have clearly indicated to the house that this group and the members of the C.C.F. throughout this country do not have a conditional loyalty to Canada, nor are they conditional Canadians. I trust, Mr. Speaker, that you will not in future hear from any member of this house any suggestion as to the loyalty of any member of any group in this house.

Mr. Speaker, may I move the adjournment of the debate?
On motion of Mr. Balcom the debate was adjourned.

Tomorrow we shall continue this debate. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has had his estimates ready for the past few days and will be awaiting the opportunity to table them at the conclusion of the debate. If that occurs, we

will go into supply. I understand that it is the wish of the house that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) should make the motion and lead off in a debate on external affairs.

Just before closing, Mr. Speaker, in view of the remarks that have just been
Business of the House made, I think I might point out to the minister that he can doubtless find ways in which the presentation of the estimates will be facilitated.
It being five minutes after eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
